item.title: One Interface, Five Geometries: An Open-Source Python Toolkit for Visualizing Wavefunctions in One-, Two-, and Three-Dimensional Infinite Potential Wells
item.description: The infinite potential well is the first quantum model students solve in closed form, and most software for it stops at one dimension. The two-and three-dimensional wells carry the concepts students find hardest: degeneracy, its symmetry origin and its lifting by anisotropy, and the topology of nodal lines and surfaces. We present the Infinite Potential Well Visualizer (IWV), an open-source Python toolkit with a Tkinter interface that treats five geometries in one workflow: the one-dimensional box, the two-dimensional rectangle, the three-dimensional box, the disk and the sphere. Each state is evaluated analytically, reported in joules and electronvolts, and rendered in six plotting modes, from line plots and heatmaps to interactive Plotly volumes. Because all geometries share one interface, one energy scale and one set of conventions, students can compare the degeneracy of a square well with its lifting in a rectangle, or the Bessel structure of the disk and sphere with the trigonometric structure of the box. We describe the physics, the numerical treatment of Bessel zeros, the visualization layer and measured performance; a 3000× 3000 grid is evaluated in 0.27 s. Every figure here is unedited output of the program’s own plotting functions.

item.title: Physically Informed Data-Driven Modeling of Low-Pressure Carburizing (LPC): A Self-Calibrating Boundary Condition for Carbon Flux
item.description: arXiv:2611.28190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper formulates an extended framework for a hybrid physically informed data-driven model of low-pressure carburizing (LPC), in which diffusive carbon transport in austenite is described by a physical equation, whereas the effective carbon flux across the gas-metal interface is treated as an unknown boundary forcing to be identified from experimental and process data. The basis for this formulation is that, in LPC, the most uncertain part of the model is not bulk diffusion but the transient surface kinetics of carbon uptake by the metal. In contrast to direct empirical relationships of the 'process regime-result' type, the proposed scheme uses machine learning as a closure operator for the boundary condition in the diffusion problem. This operator is calibrated using carbon concentration profiles, integral mass gain, surface concentration, effective case depth, and additional process measurements. Theoretically, the model is positioned as an operator-learning problem in a system constrained by a partial differential equation, physical flux constraints, inverse-problem regularization, and uncertainty quantification. The relationships between the proposed approach and physics-informed neural networks, operator learning, dynamic-system identification, boundary-operator learning, and boundary-control problems are considered. The mathematical formulation, calibration functional, identifiability conditions, preliminary tuning algorithm, and online adaptation scheme are formulated. The proposed approach is considered as a computational basis for developing interpretable digital support for LPC processes.

item.title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.29132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

item.title: CLFF: Automated Framework for Concurrent Learning Force Fields and Material Property Calculations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer an efficient paradigm for large-scale atomistic simulations with near first-principles accuracy. However, developing and deploying these potentials often involves intricate procedures that require substantial manual effort and domain expertise. In this work, we present CLFF, an open-source Python framework designed to automate concurrent learning workflows for MLIPs. CLFF integrates model training, MLIP-driven sampling, uncertainty-based candidate selection, quantum-mechanical labeling, and dataset augmentation into a unified workflow. The framework currently supports several modern graph-based MLIP architectures and is compatible with widely used computational chemistry and materials science tools. A distinguishing feature of CLFF is its ability to asynchronously distribute computational tasks across multiple heterogeneous remote computing resources, enabling users to aggregate fragmented hardware infrastructure within a single controllable workflow. In addition to concurrent learning, CLFF provides automated workflows for initial data generation and material property calculations, including phonon dispersion and potential energy surface scans. By minimizing manual intervention and enhancing reproducibility, CLFF offers a flexible platform for developing and deploying MLIPs in computational materials research.

item.title: Auditing a superconducting database built by a large language model
item.description: arXiv:2611.29445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The data on superconducting materials are published as measurements and scattered across the literature, in prose, in tables and in figures, so that gathering them into one place means reading the papers themselves. Large language models (LLMs) can read those papers, and databases built that way are appearing. The difficulty is not the reading but the trust: a number lifted out of a sentence can belong to a neighbouring compound, a computed transition temperature can be recorded without saying that it is computed, and the paper itself may be wrong. This paper describes a pipeline that extracts superconducting materials from the published literature with an LLM, checks every value against its source, and asks how far that checking goes. The pipeline proposed 19,576 records; a cascade of gates rejected 659,252 field-level extractions, 644,438 of them for want of verbatim evidence, 13,121 because the text does not attach the value to the material, and 1,693 because the source sentence reads as a calculation. The database that survives holds 3,137 material records, each with the sentence its value came from. An audit of the survivors by two independent models, on 500 records drawn in proportion to the database, shows that the gates remove the errors that are mechanical: in 93.4% of the audited records the value is in the text and the text is about the compound the record names, and 91.8% of them are measurements rather than predictions.

item.title: Fully solid-state all-2D micro-supercapacitors for on-chip energy storage
item.description: arXiv:2611.29476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating energy storage directly into microelectronic platforms remains a major challenge. Although solid-state micro-supercapacitors (MSCs) have been previously demonstrated, most still rely on liquid or solvent-containing gel electrolytes, which require additional encapsulation and complicate device integration. Here, we demonstrate wafer-scale fabrication of all-2D, fully solid-state MSCs by combining conductive Ti3C2Tz MXene electrodes with a natural vermiculite (VMT) clay solid electrolyte. Both materials are solution-processable and can be independently patterned using microelectronics compatible fabrication techniques, allowing for their integration across 4-inch Si/SiO2 wafers. The resulting devices showcase an active stack of only 28 nm thick, with an areal capacitance of 205 uF/cm2 and volumetric energy density of ~15.5 mWh/cm3. Notably, this work introduces a patterned 2D clay as a solid electrolyte in an on-chip electrochemical energy-storage device, extending the role of layered materials beyond electrodes to ion-conducting components. To investigate device behavior and degradation, we employ non-destructive imaging ellipsometry to map individual layer thicknesses and extract the spatial distribution of MXene conductivity across the chip. This approach reveals localized changes in electrode properties following prolonged electrochemical cycling, providing insight into degradation processes that are difficult to capture using conventional spatially averaged measurements. Together, these results establish a route towards fully solid-state, all-2D energy-storage devices and highlight the potential of solution-processable layered materials for integration into microelectronic systems.

item.title: AmorphGen: A Python package for amorphous structure generation with machine-learning and classical interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.29539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AmorphGen is an open-source Python package for generating and analyzing amorphous structures from a composition or a crystal. Chemically informed rules estimate initial densities and assign separation and coordination constraints. Three routes are available: random placement followed by relaxation, melt-quench from a crystal, and a hybrid route that anneals and quenches random structures. ASE provides access to classical and machine-learning potentials, with GPU batching for selected backends. Analysis tools compute coordination numbers, bond angles, rings, and X-ray or neutron structure factors for comparison with measurements. An optional interface to the FEFF code computes extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra. For amorphous Ga2O3, TiO2 and InGaZnO4, the cation coordination numbers are close to reference models and measurements, and the X-ray structure factors reproduce the main measured peaks. The EXAFS spectra for Ga2O3 and InGaZnO4 also capture the dominant first-shell features observed experimentally. The hybrid route reduces bonding defects in SiO2 and As and builds the first sharp diffraction peak of SiO2. By simplifying ensemble generation and standardizing structural assessment, AmorphGen makes it practical to compare amorphous models across compositions, potentials, and preparation routes, and to screen new amorphous compositions.

item.title: MagPot: A magnetoelastic potential generator for molecular dynamics simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetoelastic phenomena originate from the coupling between atomic displacements and magnetic degrees of freedom, and their atomistic simulation requires interatomic models in which magnetic interactions depend explicitly on interatomic distance. This paper presents MagPot, a Python program that generates Bethe-Slater parameter sets for spin-lattice molecular dynamics simulations using the SPIN package of the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS). From a compact set of material properties, the program determines the radial functions describing Heisenberg exchange and the dipole and quadrupole contributions of the two-ion N\'eel interaction. Version 1.0 supports simple-cubic, body-centred-cubic and face-centred-cubic lattices with ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations. A central feature of MagPot is its modular architecture, which allows the magnetic contribution it generates to be combined additively with a broad range of compatible non-magnetic interatomic potentials. The parameterisation workflow is assessed through equation-of-state, Curie-temperature, volume-magnetostriction, pressure-dependent magnetocrystalline-anisotropy and anisotropic-magnetoelastic tests. By automating the construction of the magnetic contribution to the interatomic model, MagPot offers a straightforward and reproducible route from material properties to LAMMPS-ready magnetic interactions, facilitating large-scale atomistic simulations of magnetoelasticity and magnetostriction, as well as physical phenomena associated with magnon-phonon coupling.

item.title: Unveiling the Complex high-pressure phases of Sodium at the Melting Curve Minimum via Data-Drive Crystal Structure Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.29889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sodium exhibits a remarkable concentration of complex crystalline phases near its melting-curve minimum, yet the atomic arrangements of several experimentally observed phases remain unresolved. Here, we combine CALYPSO crystal structure prediction with Deep Potential models developed through concurrent learning to explore this structural landscape. Searches over more than 1.6 million configurations recover the previously reported $I4/m$ structure of $tI50$ and identify candidate atomic arrangements for $oC120$ and $aP90$, together with three additional low-enthalpy structures, $tI52$, $oP72$, and $oP92$. The proposed candidates reproduce key features of the experimentally indexed cell geometries. First-principles enthalpy calculations, Gibbs free-energy comparisons, and solid--liquid coexistence simulations reveal close competition among these structures and established sodium phases. Near the calculated reference melting minimum, $tI50$ is favored over $cI16$ and $oP8$, whereas $oC120$ and $aP90$ remain closely competitive, with their relative stability sensitive to model accuracy. These results provide testable structural models for unresolved experimental phases and reveal multiple closely competing low-enthalpy configurations near sodium's melting minimum

item.title: Strain-Induced Tetragonal-to-Cubic Transition in MAPbI$_3$ from Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.30348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metal-halide perovskites are promising photovoltaic absorbers whose optoelectronic properties are highly tunable. Epitaxial strain offers a route to stabilize desirable phases, tune band gaps, and reduce energetic disorder, but rational strain engineering requires predictive models. Static, zero-temperature "strained-bulk" density functional theory (DFT) calculations, successful for oxide perovskites, neglect the dynamic disorder and anharmonicity that govern halide perovskites at ambient temperature. Here, we show that molecular dynamics (MD) based on machine-learned force fields trained on-the-fly on DFT reproduces the structural and optoelectronic response of methylammonium (MA) lead iodide (MAPbI$_3$) to epitaxial strain at 300 K. We simulate bulk and free-standing slab models across experimentally accessible biaxial strains by locking the in-plane lattice vectors in nanosecond-long simulations. We predict a tetragonal-to-cubic transition at $\sim$0.5% tensile strain, marked by $c/a = 1$ and the loss of the $a^0a^0c^-$ tilting pattern, in agreement with experiments on epitaxial MAPbI$_3$ films on KCl. MA cations retain preferential orientations in the strain-induced cubic phase, unlike in its temperature-induced counterpart. Bulk and slab models yield consistent trends, with surface effects decaying within a few octahedral layers. Band gaps computed as ensemble averages over MD snapshots blue-shift under tensile strain, consistent with experiment, whereas static calculations on averaged structures predict a red shift. Our study positions MD with constrained lattice vectors as a method for predicting finite-temperature strain phase diagrams and guiding the epitaxial design of perovskite absorbers.

item.title: Molecular Pawns on a Surface Chessboard: Computational Investigation of Nanographenes with Atomistic Methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.30917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomically precise nanographenes combine tunable electronic topology with localized, coherent spin states, making them candidate platforms for molecular quantum technologies. This review examines the multiscale theoretical framework governing these systems: the hierarchy of computational methods for describing magnetic properties, the substrate-molecule interface, on-surface synthetic kinetics, and supramolecular self-assembly. We highlight how density functional theory, automated reaction-path discovery, and spin-aware machine-learned interatomic potentials connect static electronic structure to mesoscale dynamics, and how magnetic exchange, optical excitations, and spin transport can be predicted before synthesis.

item.title: Self-consistent Floquet theory of steady-state ordering in driven open systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.30996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodically driven open systems have quasienergy bands whose steady-state occupations are set by the drive and reservoir. We formulate a self-consistent Floquet spectral theory of electronic ordering in the weak-reservoir-coupling limit, expressing the nonlinear mean-field equation and the particle-hole response in terms of quasienergies, steady-state occupations, and harmonic matrix elements that account for micromotion. We illustrate the theory in the square-lattice Hubbard model and show how the drive produces `dynamical nesting' conditions and how Floquet resonances produce \textit{hysteretic} responses due to multiple self-consistent solutions. Interestingly, we find that the hysteresis branches exhibit distinct Floquet topologies. Away from half-filling, we find that the combination of drive-induced detuning of the van Hove saddle points and the micromotion leads to the onset of switching between competing incommensurate orders.

item.title: LeIFF: A localized-electron and ion force field for coupled nuclear and electronic dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.31029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical and machine-learned interatomic potentials enable large-scale simulations by replacing electronic structure with an effective energy surface for nuclear motion. This excludes electronic dynamics, electronic excitation and energy exchange between electrons and ions. First-principles electron dynamics can describe these processes, but its computational cost restricts system sizes and simulation times. Electron force fields offer an intermediate description by treating electrons as semiclassical dynamical particles interacting with ions. We introduce the localized-electron and ion force field (LeIFF), a compact physical model for both ground state bonding and excited electron dynamics. Valence electrons are represented by spin-labeled spherical charge distributions with dynamical centers and widths. The energy combines analytic electronic kinetic, Coulomb, and dispersion terms with spline-interpolated short-range interactions fitted to a large molecular data set. The resulting energy surface describes a variety of ground state properties across diverse bonding environments and charge states. It also provides a qualitative description of electronic behavior away from equilibrium. It shows improved robustness, accuracy, and transferability relative to earlier electron force-fields. Without any solid-state training, the same model describes dielectric screening and collective electronic response in silicon. LeIFF thus opens a route to large-scale simulations of nonadiabatic processes in molecules and solids, combining chemical bonding and nonequilibrium electronic motion within a common physical framework.

item.title: Electric polarizabilities with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2611.29858v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While projector quantum Monte Carlo methods are known for producing accurate ground-state energies, the prediction of other properties that encode the electronic response to applied electric and magnetic fields has historically been challenging. In this work we demonstrate that the electric (static) polarizability tensor, which is formally a second-derivative of the energy with respect to electric fields, can be efficiently computed with phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo using a correlated sampling finite-difference strategy. With simple Hartree-Fock trial wave functions, we investigate a series of small molecules (some of which are difficult for approximate density functionals), polyacenes of increasing size, and ferrocene as a representative organometallic complex. The methodology is scalable to relatively large molecules involving thousands of basis functions, and with appropriate trial wave functions remains robust for strongly correlated electronic states, as we show for the stretched dinitrogen molecule. This work opens the door to the computation of a host of other second-order molecular properties with auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo, which will inform the ongoing search for optimal trial wave functions and extend benchmark-quality training data sets for the refinement of semi-empirical and machine learning models for quantum chemistry and molecular simulation.

item.title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.30066v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

item.title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30229v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional two-stage distillation first establishes a teacher through teacher-driven configuration exploration, a costly first stage for complex materials, and then uses its predictions to supervise students, potentially propagating teacher-label errors. Here, we propose distillation-driven teacher-student co-evolution (DICE), which uses a fast student to accelerate configuration exploration and replaces the fixed teacher-to-student sequence with alternating student and teacher updates. A representation-based support-assessment algorithm routes high-support configurations to teacher labelling and selects low-support configurations for density functional theory (DFT) calculations to update the teacher, thereby reducing the risk of teacher-label error propagation to students. Across Al2O3 (structural ceramics), yttria-stabilised zirconia (solid electrolytes) and MIL-120(Al) (a metal-organic framework), DICE develops reliable compact potentials using only 140-494 target DFT reference configurations per system; total recorded student exploration times per system are just 2.6-5.1% of the corresponding teacher-driven estimates. Combining computational efficiency with broad applicability across diverse material systems, DICE provides a practical route to developing reliable compact interatomic potentials.

item.title: Autonomous Optimization of Complex Oxides for Thermochemical Fuel Production
item.description: arXiv:2608.06877v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-step thermochemical cycles for H2O and CO2 splitting offer a promising route to sustainable fuel production. Their performance depends on redox-active oxides that undergo cyclic reduction and oxidation reactions. Achieving high thermal-to-fuel conversion efficiency requires both favorable redox thermodynamics and sufficiently rapid reaction kinetics. These requirements have shifted materials design toward complex multication oxides, including mixed-cation fluorites, perovskites, and high-entropy oxides. Developing such materials requires the simultaneous optimization of their composition, defect chemistry, phase stability, and morphology. The resulting design space is difficult to explore through sequential trial and error. Thermochemical fuel production therefore provides a compelling testbed for autonomous materials design and optimization. In this study, we first examine why redox-active complex oxides are challenging to develop owing to their multidimensional phase spaces, harsh operating conditions, and competing functional targets. We then discuss how high-throughput computation, automated synthesis, characterization, and testing, together with machine learning, can be integrated into closed-loop workflows to address these challenges. Drawing on advances from broader oxide materials research, we define a capability roadmap encompassing complex-oxide synthesis, operando characterization, robotic testing, condition-aware computation, and multi-objective optimization. Finally, we identify the key experimental, computational, data, and artificial intelligence capabilities required to build self-improving optimization platforms for materials development in thermochemical fuel production

item.title: Evaluating LLM-based AI agents integrated with materials synthesis tools: the case of atomic layer deposition
item.description: arXiv:2608.29309v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work provides an overview of the different strategies that can be used to evaluate the performance of AI models and agents based on large language models (LLMs) for materials synthesis. After providing a brief overview of the key technologies behind the current generation of AI agents based on LLMs, we summarize the different approaches to evaluating these models in the context of materials science and in particular on materials synthesis, with a specific emphasis on scenarios in which the models are directly integrated with experimental tools. We discuss evaluation strategies spanning knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, tool-use benchmarks, and closed loop benchmarks involving the interaction with experimental systems or realistic virtual tools. We use atomic layer deposition (ALD) as a case study, emphasizing how existing approaches in the literature both build from general approaches used beyond materials science and can be generalized to other materials synthesis techniques. Finally, we provide a practical evaluation framework to evaluate LLMs in the context of materials synthesis

item.title: Stochastic optimisation method for estimating large deviations
item.description: arXiv:2609.24473v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A stochastic optimisation method was recently proposed to efficiently compute large deviation functions, used in statistical physics to characterise the fluctuations of nonequilibrium systems, modelled as Markov processes. The method, called LDSTOP, combines numerical techniques from control theory and machine learning to iteratively construct the "driven process", a controlled version of the Markov process used as a model of nonequilibrium system that realises a given fluctuation or large deviation of that system in an optimal way. Compared to other methods based on spectral approximations, importance sampling, cloning or splitting, LDSTOP is simple, flexible, and scalable, as it works by simulating single trajectories that are gradually guided towards the driven process. Here, we illustrate these advantages by applying the method on the full range of Markov processes considered in applications, namely, discrete-time Markov chains, continuous-time jump processes, and diffusion processes. For each type, we define the objective function to be optimised, explain different options available for representing the driven process (using, e.g., neural networks), and provide implementation details through simple applications. With these contributions, we aim to showcase the method's efficiency, as well as its ease of use when combined with available machine learning packages, such as PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX, for simulating stochastic processes and solving high-dimensional optimisation problems.

item.title: Singlet-triplet superconductivity from repulsive interactions in a $p$-wave magnet
item.description: arXiv:2611.14609v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motivated by recent proposals of $p$-wave magnets, which host odd-parity spin splitting, we study electrons near Van Hove singularities with local repulsive interactions. We demonstrate how the symmetry of the $p$-wave spin splitting governs the competition among instabilities. Using a parquet renormalization group (pRG) analysis of a simple one-sublattice model of a $p$-wave magnet, we find that superconductivity is the leading instability over the entire phase diagram for purely repulsive interactions. The resulting superconducting state is generically a mixture of spin-singlet and spin-triplet pairing and approaches an equal-weight mixture when $T_c$ is small compared with the energy offset between each Van Hove electron and its inversion partner. Extending the pRG analysis to a more realistic two-sublattice model, we find that superconductivity remains the leading instability, while the sublattice degree of freedom leads to a competition among various singlet-triplet pairing channels and even a finite-momentum equal-spin pair-density wave. Our mechanism applies broadly to odd-parity magnets and opens a natural route to nodal topological superconductivity.

item.title: Basic introduction to Freidlin-Wentzell theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.19916v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Freidlin-Wentzell theory provides the quantitative foundation for rare, noise-induced transitions in metastable systems, predicting optimal transition paths, the exponential scaling of mean escape times, and the long-term occupancy of competing attractors. We present a pedagogical, physics-oriented review built on Feng-Kurtz's unified Hamiltonian framework: from the infinitesimal generator of a Markov process we derive the Hamiltonian, the Lagrangian and action via Legendre-Fenchel duality, and the quasi-potential. The same formalism covers weak-noise diffusions, Markov jump processes, interacting particle systems, and nonequilibrium stochastic fields. We show how broken detailed balance separates forward and reverse transition paths, and how W-graphs construct multi-attractor landscapes. Finally, we connect the theory to numerical methods, including ordered upwind methods, geometric minimum action algorithms, and neural-network parameterizations, and provide an accompanying GPU-accelerated Python package.

item.title: The phase diagram of fluid hydrogen near melting from machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on quantum Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2611.25178v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dissociation of molecular hydrogen increasing temperature or pressure may either occur gradually or abruptly, via a phase transition. Despite considerable experimental and theoretical efforts, the phase diagram of dense hydrogen at temperatures above solid melting is not precisely known. Here, we perform classical and quantum Path Integral molecular dynamics simulations of dense hydrogen using two machine-learned interatomic potentials both trained on quantum Monte Carlo energies and forces. The resulting phase diagram is constructed using state-of-the-art techniques. Both models show a first-order phase transition from the molecular to the atomic liquid terminating in critical points whose locations were determined using finite-size scaling techniques. Triple points, located at the highest temperature of the melting curve, are found at the intersection of the liquid-liquid lines with the melting curve and should lead to clear signatures in ramp compression experiments.

item.title: momipy: A time-resolved momentum microscopy data analysis workflow
item.description: arXiv:2611.25888v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photoemission momentum microscopy is an emerging approach to photoelectron spectroscopy that is transforming electronic band structure mapping at both laboratory-based and large-scale facilities. Its extension to time-resolved measurements has recently enabled major advances, ranging from the femtosecond imaging of exciton wavefunctions to dark-field photoelectron microscopy of light-induced dynamics and strong light-matter interactions. However, the rapid acquisition of high-dimensional data sets (including electron in-plane momenta $k_x$ and $k_y$, kinetic energy $E_\mathrm{kin}$, time $\Delta t$, and more) poses substantial challenges for data handling and analysis. A typical workflow encompasses data acquisition, exploratory visualization, calibration and targeted feature extraction, with data management ideally guided by FAIR principles. Here, we present momipy, a Python package that streamlines the momentum microscopy data analysis workflow efficiently and at low computational cost. Among other features, momipy provides interactive 4D data visualization, energy and momentum calibration, space-charge correction, and a broad selection of multidimensional data analysis routines, including binning, momentum-map extraction and time-, energy- and momentum-resolved model fitting. momipy is accompanied by a selection of interactive example scripts, supporting adoption of momipy by both experienced researchers and users new to momentum microscopy.

item.title: More Bang for the Buck: Improving the Inference of Large Language Models at a Fixed Budget using Reset and Discard (ReD)
item.description: arXiv:2601.21522v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The performance of large language models (LLMs) on verifiable tasks is usually measured by pass@k, the probability of solving a problem correctly at least once in k trials. At a fixed budget, a more suitable metric is coverage@cost, the average number of unique problems solved as a function of the total number of attempts. We connect the two metrics and show that the empirically-observed power-law behavior in pass@k leads to a sublinear growth of the coverage@cost (diminishing returns). To solve this problem, we propose Reset-and-Discard (ReD), a query method of LLMs that increases coverage@cost for a given budget, regardless of the pass@k form. Moreover, given a pass@k, we can quantitatively predict the savings in the total number of attempts using ReD. If pass@k is not available for the model, ReD can infer its power-law exponent. Experiments across coding (HumanEval), math (GSM8K), and reasoning (MMLU-Pro) benchmarks, as well as real GitHub issues solved by a coding agent (SWE-bench Lite), demonstrate that ReD substantially reduces the required attempts, tokens, and USD cost to reach a desired coverage, while also offering an efficient way to measure inference power-laws. ReD's advantage is maintained for imperfect verifiers.

item.title: Stagewise and interpretable emergence of inside-outside computation in Transformer-based language models
item.description: arXiv:2611.14221v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Variability in syntactic structure and parsing ambiguity are fundamental aspects of natural language which modern LLMs have to learn to deal with proficiently. Previous "post-mortem" studies have shown that fully trained Transformers indeed approximate canonical parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but little is established theoretically about how this is actually learned. Here, we make a first step towards addressing this by studying the learning dynamics in synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology. The stagewise learning curves are fully interpretable, in the sense that all of the loss stages a) can be computed analytically, and b) can be clearly associated to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable, which allows to lift ambiguity and utilize information from wider contexts. By probing representations, we visualize the emergence of inside-outside computation across depth and during training: while during early stages local (bigram/trigram) information is used and involves only a few initial layers, gradually the Transformer develops an encoder-decoder structure where the most abstract latent information is encoded in the middle, and the latter half of the network is used to progressively refine the final token prediction. This organization of computation is reminiscent of findings in real-world LLMs, and importantly applies here to a synthetic model which allows full analytical control of the data statistics, thus opening the door to theoretical progress.

item.title: Construction of a Deployable Closure Model for the Transport of Turbulence Dissipation Rate with Hard-Constrained Physics-Informed Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.23539v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a hard-constrained physics-informed machine learning (PIML) method for constructing a deployable closure model for the transport of turbulence dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals. This coupling allows us to learn the closure without using reference closure values as training targets. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We study decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) and learn $\psi$, the closure function governing dissipation rate decay, from trajectories obtained in experiments and direct numerical simulations. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. The framework reduces the root mean square of the closure variation across ten random seeds by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number $Re_{\lambda_g}$ and can be exported as a standalone C function.

item.title: Assessing the Stability, Synthesizability, and Transport Properties of Aliovalently-Doped Multivalent Solid Electrolytes
Hierarchical Theory of Chemical Bond: From the Schrödinger Equation to Aromaticity and Homochirality
item.description: Chemical bonds are described by many complementary concepts whose relationships and limits are often unclear. Building on the four empirical directions of two-center bonding identified by machine learning in the preceding article, we formulate a hierarchical theory of the chemical bond from the electronic Schrödinger equation. Because the energy is an exact functional of the one- and two-particle reduced density matrices, partitioning these matrices among fragments (atoms, functional groups, or molecules) organizes bonding information by the connectivity of the fragments and by its kind: one-particle coherence, electron correlation, or response. Two-fragment quantities (bond index, covalent–ionic coordinate, bond polarity, and π fraction) describe bond multiplicity and polarization, whereas correlated bond cleavage separates the loss of electron sharing from the growth of static correlation, and hydrogen bonding and dispersion are distinguished by their coherence and cumulant signatures. Three-center delocalization is determined by pair blocks of the density matrix, but maximum-entropy calculations reveal three-orbital correlation beyond all pair information. Ring delocalization likewise differs from aromatic response: current-coupled excitations govern aromaticity, Baird reversal, and the collective response of fused rings. Finally, an exact expansion over all 64 stereoisomers of two hexaalanine helices attributes 99.9% and 98.6% of the variance of their energies to one-residue fields imposed by a helix of fixed handedness, a quantitative form of the principle of chirality hierarchy. Each level of the hierarchy is thus defined by the information that the levels below it do not contain.

item.title: Can we teach generative artificial intelligence the design language of engineered living materials?
item.description: Díaz Lantada et al. present an ontology and codification for engineered living materials (ELMs), illustrating their applicability as classification tools leading to the current knowledge graph of this emergent field. Furthermore, the synergistic application of the ontology for co-designing novel ELMs with a generative artificial intelligence is explored and demonstrated.

item.title: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03836-z

Anthropic and OpenAI’s language models can design proteins and predict their sequences and structures — capabilities previously seen only in specialized AI tools.

item.title: Scaffold-guided generative AI for Type I photosensitizer design in hypoxic photodynamic therapy
item.description: Type I photosensitizers (PSs) are attractive for photodynamic therapy (PDT) of hypoxic tumors, but their development is limited by empirical modification and library screening. Here, we develop a scaffold-guided generative AI framework that couples Type I-specific prediction with controllable molecular generation for prospective PS design. AI-assisted literature mining and molecular structure recognition were first used to construct a curated data set of 1338 PSs. Subsequently, we developed BiCAM-PS, a cross-attention model integrating molecular graphs, fingerprints, and physicochemical descriptors, which achieved an accuracy of 93.3% and an ROC–AUC of 0.9633 for Type I classification under the random split. We further established PSGenerator, a scaffold decorator that generates structurally diverse molecules around predefined attachment sites, enabling prediction-guided exploration of Type I PS chemical space. Using a redesigned tetracyclic scaffold as a test case, the framework prioritized six synthetically accessible candidates, all of which experimentally exhibited Type I characteristics. Among them, A1 showed efficient radical ROS generation, strong photostability, mitochondrial localization, and potent photodynamic activity under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions, markedly suppressing 4T1 tumor growth in vivo without obvious systemic toxicity. Together, this work establishes a data-driven framework that advances Type I PS discovery from empirical molecular modification and library screening toward prospective generative design.

item.title: Molecular Dynamics Assessment of Monomer-level Approximations in Density Functional Theory of Polymer Electrolytes: From Bulk to Ceramic Interfaces
item.description: Determining the interactions and chain or ion dynamics in the bulk polymer phase and at polymer-ceramic interfaces is crucial for next-generation polymer-ceramic composite electrolyte design, where polymer chain dynamics and interfacial structure strongly influence ion coordination and transport. In this work, we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate Li+ coordination and interfacial structure in poly(lithium sulfonyl (trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide methacrylate) (pMTFSILi) and Li0.5La0.5TiO3 (LLTO) systems. Firstly, single chain and bulk polymer-only MD simulations are used to investigate the impact of chain length and tacticity in the MD structure build on ion coordination in the polymer. For these MD simulations of the polymer phase, it is shown that DFT polymer fragment approximations underestimate ion binding in the bulk, but that Li+ energetics are likely controlled by repeat unit chemistry as opposed to chain architecture and conformation, which is qualitatively captured in DFT models.Secondly, DFT calculations of monomer and dimer adsorption on LLTO surfaces are then done to establish reference interfacial geometries and local coordination environments. These DFT structures are used to validate the cross-interactions between polymer and ceramic atom types used in the classical MD simulations by comparing partial radial distribution functions, which exhibit a consistent first-shell coordination environment between DFT and MD. These indicate accurate reproduction of local interfacial chemistry by modeling these cross-interactions as mostly electrostatic (Coulombic-dominated). Thirdly, we build on this validation to perform classical MD simulations of an extended atomistic bulk polymer and LLTO interface to examine structural organization beyond isolated polymer fragment adsorption. The results of these simulations demonstrate that the validated MD interatomic potential, specifically the cross-interactions between the polymer and ceramic atom types, captures key features of Li+ coordination at the polymer-ceramic interface and enables extension from simplified polymer fragment adsorption models to realistic interfacial structures. The resulting multiscale framework thus provides a foundation for future atomic-scale computational studies on ion transport and interfacial dynamics in polymer-ceramic composite electrolytes.

item.title: Building a grain-boundary machine-learning force field by reactive sampling and data curation, and its application to large-scale grain-boundary transport in Li6PS5X (X =Cl, Br)
item.description: General-purpose machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) achieve near-DFT accuracy for equilibrium properties, yet their reliability for rare, non-equilibrium events—such as Li migration in grain-boundary (GB) corescannot be judged from static error metrics alone. Here we present a datageneration, curation, and validation framework that turns this judgment into a routine check, demonstrated on argyrodite Li6PS5X. Reactive-path sampling (ODPMD) concentrated in the transition region yields configurations far from the existing data (44% novel vs. 4% for intact-phase frames), which are screened by a physical-consistency filter and selected by stratified sampling in a MatterSim descriptor space. Fine-tuning MatterSim on this compact, regime-balanced data set reduces held-out DFT Li-migration barrier errors from 44meV to 32meV MAE (median 25meV), mainly in the rate-limiting high-barrier tail, while retaining bulk properties. MD on GB models of up to 4344 atoms shows, for both models, a mild activation penalty (∆Ea = +50–80 meV) that suppresses Li diffusion mainly at low temperature (DGB/Dbulk ≈ 0.46 at 500 K vs. 0.59 for the universal model at the ordered boundary) but is nearly invisible at the 700–800 K commonly simulated; electric-field-driven non-equilibrium MD corroborates this weak blocking. The universal model thus captures the qualitative physics, but its quantitative reliability can be established only by validating local barri-

item.title: Targeted Versus Broad Descriptor Generation: A Case Study in Primary Sulfonamide Acidity
item.description: As machine learning becomes increasingly common in chemistry, an important question is how chemical knowledge should guide molecular featurization. Here, a simple rule-based acidity score for primary sulfonamides was developed through the selection, encoding, and weighting of molecular features using open-access RDKit tools. Initial feature weights were assigned based on established chemical principles governing acidity and refined by comparison with a DFT-derived ranking of 44 compounds, achieving Spearman’s ρ = 0.779. Applied unchanged to an independent dataset of 32 experimentally measured pKa values, the score showed strong agreement with acidity rankings (ρ = 0.794, τb = 0.611) and compared favorably with QupKake, a machine-learning pKa estimator. These results suggest that simple structure-based descriptors can approximate DFT-and experimentally derived acidity trends without repeated quantum-chemical calculations. Further data-driven optimization of feature weights improved agreement with the DFT development data but worsened performance on the experimental dataset. A broader feature-generation approach employing 150 automatically generated RDKit descriptors likewise reduced performance on the experimental dataset. These findings highlight the broader potential of using established chemical principles to guide the development of simple, accessible, and interpretable molecular representations.

item.title: Spectral functions of an extended antiferromagnetic $S=\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice
item.description:
Author(s): Markus Drescher, Laurens Vanderstraeten, Roderich Moessner, and Frank Pollmann

Quantum spin liquids are exotic phases of matter that do not form magnetic order, even at zero temperature. Instead, a single spin flip breaks apart into two independent emergent fractionalized particles, leaving a distinctive continuum in neutron-scattering spectra. Here, using GPU-accelerated dynamical matrix-product-state simulations, the authors compute such spectra for a frustrated triangular-lattice antiferromagnet with new levels of accuracy. The results support the existence of two spin-liquid phases, a U(1) Dirac spin liquid and a chiral spin liquid.
