item.title: Charge‐Regulated Ion Transport in Cyclodextrin‐Functionalized Nanochannels for Chiral Sensing
item.description: Small, EarlyView.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: Correlating CO2 reduction selectivity with ML-quantified morphology of surface Cu and cracks in gas diffusion electrodes
item.description: Gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) enable Cu-catalyzed CO2 electroreduction (CO2RR) at industrially relevant current densities, but their porous, multicomponent architecture evolves during operation, affecting selectivity and stability in poorly understood ways. We use machine learning clustering of post-mortem electron micrographs to quantify the morphology of surface Cu and cracks of three types of copper-carbon paper GDEs at different stages of CO2RR selectivity decay. Pixels are grouped by lightness to identify bright regions associated with agglomerated or rough Cu catalyst and dark regions associated with cracks that extend through the Cu layer in the gas diffusion layer. For each class, we quantify the average patch area, average total area, and average boundary length. These descriptors correlate with C2H4, CO, and H2 Faradaic efficiencies at least as strongly as conventional observables such as electrode resistance and potential, and gas or liquid pressure. Larger average Cu patch areas correlate with lower C2H4 and CO selectivity in nanoparticle electrodes, consistent with detrimental nanoparticle agglomeration. In contrast, both larger average Cu patches and a larger total area of rough Cu correlate with higher C2H4 and CO selectivity in sputtered electrodes, consistent with a larger electrochemically active Cu surface area. Across electrode types, larger crack patches are associated with higher C2H4 and CO selectivity relative to H2, consistent with cracks providing preferential drainage pathways that limit flooding. Without a Nafion overcoat, larger crack patches combined with a smaller total crack area are associated with higher C2H4 and CO selectivity, whereas Nafioncoated electrodes retain selectivity despite more extensive cracking. Our findings identify morphological parameters that can guide the design of more selective and stable CO2RR electrodes.

item.title: Learning from formulation revisions for closed-loop electrolyte optimization
item.description: Electrolyte design for high-energy batteries remains largely empirical, as compositional changes introduce complex trade-offs among ion transport, solvation and interfacial stability. Although data-driven approaches have advanced electrolyte property prediction and candidate optimization, improvements in individual properties do not necessarily translate into better performance in working batteries. Meanwhile, empirical knowledge about how researchers have modified electrolyte formulations to address specific design challenges remains largely untapped. Here we develop a framework that reconstructs literature-reported formulation changes as directed transitions. Within this framework, the Transition-grounded Revision Agent for Closed-loop Electrolyte Optimization (TRACE) learns composition- and objective-dependent modification preferences, grounds molecular proposals, and uses physics-based feedback to guide successive revisions. Starting from a conventional LiPF6-based EMC/PC electrolyte, the framework explores additive and solvent modifications and identifies an FEMC/TFPC (8:2) formulation with increased anion participation in Li+ solvation while maintaining ionic conductivity. In 5-Ah pouch cells, the capacity decay rate decreases from 0.085% to 0.042% per cycle. Under a separate leanelectrolyte configuration, high-energy cell achieves 509 Wh kg-1 and retains 498 Wh kg-1 after 200 cycles. These findings show how historical formulation experience can be transformed into evidence-grounded, feedback-guided decisions for electrolyte design.

item.title: Selective Lanthanide-Binding Peptides: Molecular Insights into Binding Affinity and Selectivity
item.description: Rare earth elements (REEs), including the lanthanides, are essential to clean-energy technologies, semiconductors, electric vehicles, turbines, and other advanced materials that exploit their luminescent, magnetic, and catalytic properties. Current REE separation methods, however, suffer from poor selectivity, high solvent use, and environmental burden, which motivates greener and more selective strategies. Here we combine fluorescence binding measurements, molecular dynamics, enhanced-sampling calculations, descriptor analysis, and machine learning to determine how lanthanide-binding tag (LBT) peptides discriminate among trivalent REE cations in aqueous solution. The peptides operate in two binding regimes. For larger, lighter REEs, affinity is governed primarily by ion size, solvation, solvent accessibility, and non-bonded electrostatic interactions in a loosely coordinated binding pocket. For smaller, heavier REEs, the pocket contracts, and steric crowding, ligand–ligand electrostatic repulsion, and backbone torsional strain increasingly oppose further stabilization. Correlation analyses with sequence-derived, solvation, ligation, and conformational descriptors support this dichotomy. Analysis of selected LBT1-derived variants yields design rules: terminal charge tunes absolute affinity, ligating-residue geometry controls productive electrostatic coordination, a gatekeeper residue regulates water access and steric closure, and terminal residue hydrophobicity modulates amphiphilicity while preserving lanthanide-size sensitivity. Finally, classifiers trained on 37,041 sequences predict coarse Tb3+ affinity classes from a few bioinformatic descriptors, including disorder propensity, charge, amphiphilicity, and hydrophobicity, whereas predicting relative affinity across the full lanthanide series remains sensitive to solvation and binding-pocket remodeling. These results provide a molecular framework for engineering peptides for selective REE recovery and separation.

item.title: Accuracy and Limits of Pretrained Interatomic Potentials Across Molecular Reaction Pathways
item.description: Foundation models of machine-learning interatomic potentials are now used to search for reaction pathways, but the common reactive test sets share structures with the training data for several of these models. We compare energies and forces from fifteen pretrained models with DFT single-point values at fixed GFN2-xTB-derived geometries from 9,017 gas-phase reaction pathways in DORTS-9K, a separately generated dataset, and extend the comparison to seventeen models for the reactions that contain only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen (CHNO). Models trained on molecular data are the most accurate, and the best of them, UMA-M OMol, has a median force RMSE of 0.018 eV Å⁻¹ and reproduces 96% of the 3,713 CHNO barriers within 1 kcal mol⁻¹. Force errors increase from the endpoints to the transition-state anchors for all molecular models, nearly doubling for UMA-M OMol. Across the 38 CHNO reactions with the largest UMA-M OMol barrier errors, all models except AIMNet2 and AIMNet2-RXN underestimate the DFT barriers by 6.5–85.2% across models and reactions. These include hydrogen transfers involving nitrous acid and an azide/isocyanate template.

item.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
item.description: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

item.title: Hierarchical formulation optimization for accelerated discovery of chemical mixtures
item.description: The design of chemical mixtures, or formulations, is a critical yet challenging aspect of materials science due to the combinatorial explosion of possible ingredient and composition variations. Traditional trial-and-error methods are costly, especially when optimizing for multiple target properties concurrently. To accelerate formulation discovery, we developed a multiparameter, hierarchical optimization framework that integrates high-throughput machine learning (ML) predictions with sophisticated search algorithms. The optimization workflow is data-source agnostic, functioning with both experimental and simulated inputs. We first benchmarked optimization algorithms using a large, self-consistent dataset of simulated solvent mixtures to isolate algorithmic search efficiency from experimental noise. We then rigorously benchmarked various optimization algorithms. For composition optimization, the differential evolution algorithm was identified as the most robust and efficient method, rapidly identifying optimal compositions with minimal ML prediction calls. For ingredient selection, a genetic algorithm (GA) significantly outperformed brute force, random, and Bayesian optimization approaches, finding a much higher proportion of top-performing formulations with the fewest samples. By coupling GA for ingredient selection with differential evolution for composition refinement, the hierarchical workflow successfully maximized a multiparameter optimization score across diverse materials applications, including minimizing solvent viscosity, maximizing drug solubility, and maximizing motor octane number. Representative optimized formulation candidates were subsequently evaluated using classical molecular dynamics simulations to independently validate the property trends predicted by the data-driven optimization approach. This work highlights a robust, intelligent, and rapid computer-aided workflow for navigating the complex design space of chemical mixtures, minimizing the need for extensive physical experimentation and accelerating the discovery of high-performing, tailored formulations.

item.title: Fully Automated Discovery of Phase Diagrams Using Agentic Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classifying phases of matter and mapping out phase diagrams are central problems in physics. Recently, machine learning techniques have emerged as promising tools for phase classification, ranging from supervised learning to various unsupervised methods. However, these techniques provide limited qualitative insight into the discovered phases, typically work only for specific system classes, and do not by themselves efficiently map out the phase diagram. Autonomously constructing the phase diagram of a general system purely from measurements, without prior knowledge of the system, while also yielding qualitative understanding of the phases, remains an open task. In this work, we introduce Phasonaut, a two-agent framework that leverages the tool-use capabilities and broad knowledge of large language models (LLMs) to drive an active learning loop that constructs phase diagrams of physical systems and provides interpretations of the discovered phases. Starting from scratch, it iteratively selects and performs measurements, analyzes the resulting data, and segments the parameter domain into the phases it discovers. Phasonaut recovers the phase diagrams of classical and quantum spin systems to substantial precision. In the future, this framework could enable rapid exploration of systems with unknown phase diagrams, including in autonomously driven experiments.

item.title: Prediction of lattice thermal conductivity of half-Heusler compounds by machine learning and transfer-function calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.26788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-throughput searches for half-Heusler thermoelectrics increasingly rely on lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa_L$) from first-principles calculations, or from machine-learning models trained on them. These calculations describe an ideal single crystal, whereas measurements are made on polycrystalline samples, in which grain boundaries and defects scatter heat as well. The resulting gap between calculated and measured $\kappa_L$ has been noted for individual compounds but not, to our knowledge, quantified across a materials class, so the values used for screening carry an unknown, systematic bias. Here we quantify and correct this bias for cubic half-Heusler compounds with 18 valence electrons. Using a curated literature corpus that keeps calculated and measured values apart, we show that calculations overestimate measured $\kappa_L$ in most bonding families, and that the excess shrinks with temperature. Scattering by defects, added to the intrinsic scattering between lattice vibrations, would give such a trend, but the data do not single out one cause. A simple transfer function with this temperature dependence removes the median offset, and refitting its magnitude within a bonding family lowers the median error further, though not consistently compound by compound. Combined with a machine-learning model that predicts the calculated value from crystal structure, and tested on chemistries withheld from all fitting, the method predicts measured $\kappa_L$ in this class about as closely as independent laboratories agree with one another, and provides testable predictions for compounds not yet measured.

item.title: Tailoring Phonon Transport in Bi-based Quaternary Half-Heusler alloys for Thermoelectric Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.27234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quaternary half-Heuslers (QHHs) are substitutionally disordered derivatives of conventional halfHeusler (HH) compounds, which offer a potential route to modify phonon transport and enhance thermoelectric performance. Here, we investigate the thermoelectric properties of the quaternary half-Heuslers ZrHfRh2Bi2, ZrHfIr2Bi2, Zr2RhIrBi2, and Hf2RhIrBi2 using first-principles calculations and anharmonic lattice dynamics. Among four compounds, ZrHfRh2Bi2 and Zr2RhIrBi2 exhibit semiconducting electronic structure and others are semimetallic in nature. Both the semiconducting compounds show favorable electronic transport properties. However, quaternary substitution substantially modifies the phonon dispersion, lowering the average phonon group velocity by about 17-22% relative to the parent compounds while leaving the anharmonic scattering rates comparable. The combination of high power factor and low kl results in high thermoelectric performance, with maximum ZT values of 2.28 and 2.18 at 1000 K for p-type ZrHfRh2Bi2 and Zr2RhIrBi2, respectively, with maximum thermoelectric power conversion efficiency 16.3% for p-type ZrHfRh2Bi2. Further reducing the grain size enhances the thermoelectric performance, with maximum ZT values of 2.51 and 2.58 at 1000 K for p-type ZrHfRh2Bi2 and Zr2RhIrBi2, respectively, at a grain size of 30 nm. Our results demonstrate that combining substitutional disorder with grain boundary engineering, provides an effective strategy to enhance the thermoelectric performance of HH compounds.

item.title: From non-universal spectra at the RS-RSB transition to the universal $\omega^4$ regime inside the glassy phase
item.description: arXiv:2611.27564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The universal low-frequency nonphononic density of states $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{G}(\omega)\sim\omega^4$ is a robust feature of structural glasses, yet its origin remains poorly understood. Here we investigate this question using the mean-field KHGPS model of interacting anharmonic oscillators. We show that the universal quartic spectrum is deeply rooted in the glassy, replica-symmetry-broken (RSB) phase, whereas the gapless density of states found at the boundary of the replica-symmetric (RS) phase is non-universal and depends sensitively on the details of the quenched disorder. We formulate a simplified variant of the KHGPS model that allows us to characterize the crossover between these two regimes and provides a physical interpretation of the associated crossover frequency scale. We further show that the conventional, spin-glass-like, continuous RS-RSB transition, accompanied by diverging susceptibilities, can be suppressed by an appropriate choice of the quenched disorder, allowing for a discontinuous RS-RSB transition even in the absence of an external field. Our results establish a direct connection between the emergence of the universal $\omega^4$ spectrum and the glassy phase, and provide a simple framework for exploring the low-temperature properties of glasses and the soft localized excitations that emerge from bistable local potentials.

item.title: Physical Learning for Autonomous Tuning of Spin Qubits in Electrostatically Defined Quantum Dots
item.description: arXiv:2611.27140v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tuning electrostatically defined quantum dots remains a primary bottleneck in the scalability of semiconductor spin qubits. While existing solutions rely on machine learning algorithms, these approaches require global information, introduce latency bottlenecks, and tax the limited cooling power available at cryogenic stages. Here, we demonstrate an FPGA-in-the-loop learning paradigm that bypasses digital computing overhead by utilizing multiplexed gradient descent (MGD) for tuning. Implemented on an FPGA and an emulated quantum dot device, our system autonomously tracks environmental drift, dynamically recovers from discrete charge jumps, and maintains steady-state stabilization in low signal-to-noise ratio regimes, without prior knowledge of the device's cross-capacitance matrix. The system also navigates the charge-stability landscape to stabilize the quantum dot around optimal operating points. These results demonstrate a ``compute-in-place'' platform, with a logic and power footprint suited to future cryo-CMOS integration, that provides autonomous stabilization of quantum dots at desired operating points, creating an auto-tuning system for spin qubits that is resilient to electrostatic drifts, changing noise profiles, and two-level fluctuations.

item.title: geodesiq: a Python package for geometric diabatic-adiabatic optimal state transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.27535v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce the geodesiq Python package, which implements a geometric framework for shaping control pulses that achieve high-fidelity state transfer in multilevel quantum systems. The underlying method combines adiabatic and diabatic control into a single metric, suppressing unwanted excitations while allowing selected diabatic passages. Finding the pulse thereby reduces to solving a single first-order ordinary differential equation. We explain how to use geodesiq and illustrate its use explicitly with Landau-Zener transitions, spin-qubit initialization, adiabatic many-body ground-state preparation, and a diabatic-adiabatic transfer in a four-level system.

item.title: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.27618v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.

item.title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

item.title: Rippled graphene pores as fluidic memristive devices with synaptic and neuromorphic functionalities
item.description: arXiv:2604.19228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nanofluidic memristive devices work with nanoscale pores and ions dissolved in water, which harness the ionic memory effect aiming to store and process information. These devices share the same charge carriers as biological systems and bring hope for better emulating the neural functions and developing ionic circuits for neuromorphic applications. Specially, theory and experiments suggest that nanoconfinement is essential for inducing a memory effect, which places limit on the pore size to nm-scale or smaller. Such devices are difficult to scale up with precision and operate with long-term stability. Here, we show that a micrometer size pore, generally expected to exhibit a linear ion transport, can display a pronounced memory effect, if its rim is wrapped by strongly curved and tightly stacked graphene. We attribute the observation to slow ion dynamics confined in the rippled graphene edges. The devices are easy to scale up and integrate into fluidic circuits. The memory effect is ion-selective and exhibits long endurance comparable to the lifetime of synaptic proteins, which enables reversible modification of the conductance states using programmable voltage spikes and various electrolytes over a long time, akin to biological synaptic plasticity. Thanks to this plasticity, our devices and their integrated circuits enable storing, transmitting and processing information with high reliability, fidelity and accuracy, as evidenced in the identification of both greyscale and color images, and in the real-time analysis of emulated neural signals. Our results highlight nanoscale morphology of the pore wall as an important parameter regulating ion transport and indicate that the stringent nanoconfinement for ionic memory can be lifted from restricting the pore size to designing its rim structure. The devices and their integrated circuits may find use in ionic neuromorphic applications.

item.title: AutoDFT: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous DFT Calculations
item.description: arXiv:2605.26179v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) serves as the basis for computational discovery in materials science and chemistry, yet each calculation demands extensive human effort: adjusting algorithms when convergence stalls, revising plans when unexpected physics emerges, and inserting steps as intermediate results reshape the problem. Existing LLM-based agents automate only the initial planning stage, producing a full execution plan upfront and leaving all subsequent adaptation to hand-crafted rules. As a result, these workflows remain fragile, do not generalize well beyond pre-planned scenarios, and often require expert intervention when failures or unexpected intermediate results require changes to the calculation path. Here, we introduce AutoDFT, a closed-loop multi-agent framework that embeds LLM reasoning into every stage of the DFT lifecycle, where a strategic planner produces a skeletal plan of step objectives; a step planner generates numerical parameters just in time from preceding results; and a monitor-recover-reflect cycle diagnoses failures, repairs them, and revises the plan when the evidence justifies it. We demonstrate both breadth and depth: breadth on VASPBench, a purpose-built benchmark spanning 34 tasks and 9 DFT calculation types, where AutoDFT achieves 94.1% task-level success with GPT-5.2; and depth on established materials databases, where AutoDFT produces quantitatively reliable property predictions across electronic, magnetic, and energetic properties. By closing the loop between planning and execution, AutoDFT enables experimentalists without deep computational expertise to obtain reliable first-principles results. Our code is available at https://github.com/penghui-yang/AutoDFT.

item.title: Energy spectra and cascade in the spin turbulence of a driven spinor Bose-Einstein condensate
item.description: arXiv:2606.00766v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the spin-interaction energy spectrum of spin turbulence in a driven spinor Bose-Einstein condensate. Continuous spin driving of a spin-1 condensate produces a nonequilibrium steady state with spatially fluctuating magnetization. We observe a power-law scaling consistent with the $-7/3$ exponent predicted for spin-wave turbulence, which persists across our full range of drive strengths despite substantial changes in the spectral anisotropy. After switching off the drive, we track the free-decay evolution and find evidence consistent with a direct cascade of spin-interaction energy toward higher wavenumbers. These results establish an energy-spectral hallmark of spin turbulence and enable quantitative studies of cascade dynamics in spinor superfluids.

item.title: Reactivity-Informed Machine Learning for Performance Prediction and Design Space Exploration of Alkali-Activated Slag
item.description: arXiv:2606.06765v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Establishing quantitative relationships among mix design, raw material properties, curing conditions, and performance remains a long-standing challenge in cementitious materials, particularly for alkali-activated materials with variable precursor and activator chemistry. Here, we curated the largest literature-derived alkali-activated slag (AAS) dataset to date, comprising over 3100 compressive strength records, 155 chemically distinct ground granulated blast-furnace slags (GGBSs), and 24 attributes incorporating precursor chemistry, fineness, and reactivity. Multiple machine learning (ML) algorithms were benchmarked across progressively enriched feature scenarios, demonstrating that integrating GGBS compositions, fineness, curing conditions, and specimen geometry improves predictive performance. The average metal oxide dissociation energy (AMODE), a physically interpretable representation of precursor reactivity, provides a compact alternative descriptor to explicit oxide compositions while enabling comparable predictive performance. Model interpretation revealed physically consistent trends from heterogeneous data, including non-monotonic effects of Na2O dosage and silicate modulus, reduced predicted strength at higher water content and larger specimen size, and coupled oxide-level effects more coherently represented by AMODE than by individual oxide contents. Statistically constrained design space exploration reveals reactivity-dependent trade-offs among strength, embodied CO2 emissions, and cost. The design maps identify high-strength regions with substantially lower CO2 emissions than OPC-based references at similar cost. Overall, this work demonstrates how reactivity-informed ML can extract physically meaningful trends from heterogeneous AAS data and guide source-dependent binder design. The curated dataset is publicly accessible to support advances in cement and concrete research.

item.title: Mapping the Growth of Two-Dimensional $\pi$-Conjugated Polymers on Au(111): Organometallic Intermediates and Edge Terminations
item.description: arXiv:2606.27512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kagome lattices provide an exciting space for the exploration of graphene-like $\pi$-conjugated molecular systems with flat bands. Using heterotriangulene-derived precursors, along with an on-surface Ullmann coupling process, makes growing polymers with Kagome lattices accessible and straightforward. Here, we use scanning tunneling microscopy alongside high-resolution atomic force microscopy to examine the evolution of tribromotrioxaazatriangulene on Au(111) into ordered, covalent films. Using density functional theory and scanning probe methods, we find previously unreported organometallic intermediate states involving Au adatoms incorporated within the growing polymer lattice. We also find that a majority of polymer edges remain brominated up to 250 $^{\circ}$C and a large number of edges bonded to Au adatoms coordinated to an adjacent bromine atom. These observations suggest that residual bromine could play a role in stabilizing the polymer edges to Au adatoms and thereby influence the growth pathways that lead to ordered Kagome polymer lattices.

item.title: Agentic programs: an emerging form of scientific software in computational materials science
item.description: arXiv:2609.00795v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Computational materials science has traditionally delegated algorithmic tasks to computers while leaving scientific judgments to humans. In this Perspective, we argue that agent harnesses built on large language models (LLMs) enable an emerging form of scientific software, agentic programs, integrating deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, task-specific verification, episodic maturation, and complete delegation. We illustrate these characteristics through DeMARS, which constructs atomistic models from experimentally measured disordered crystal structures.

item.title: Stereochemistry-aware classification and regression of polymer melting temperatures
item.description: Milrod et al. develop stereochemistry-aware machine learning models to predict polymer melting temperatures through classification and regression. The best classifier achieves an AUPRC of 0.98 and an AUROC of 0.96 on a held-out test set. The best regressor achieves an R2 of 0.90 and an MAE of 13.2°C.

item.title: Glassy metal-organic frameworks as fillers enabling all-solid-state lithium metal batteries operating from room to elevated temperatures
item.description:

item.title: Interfacial Transition-Metal Reduction, Surface Oxygen Depletion and LiNbO3 Protection in NCM622/Li6PS5Cl Cathodes Resolved by In Situ Nanoscale XPEEM
item.description: Degradation at the cathode-solid electrolyte interface limits high-energy-density sulfide-based allsolid-state batteries. For Ni-rich LiNi0.6Mn0.2Co0.2O2 (NCM622), cathode surface reduction and electrolyte oxidation are coupled through interfacial (electro-)chemical reactions. Although LiNbO3 coatings are known to mitigate interfacial resistance growth, their effect on this coupling during operation remains unclear. Here, we combine operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and in situ X-ray photoemission electron microscopy (XPEEM) to follow the chemical evolution of the NCM622 surface and interfaces with Li6PS5Cl (LPSCl) with depth sensitivity and nanoscale spatial resolution. Already at open-circuit potential, reduced transition-metals, oxygendeficient domains and sulfate species co-localize where NCM622 particles contact LPSCl. Upon high-voltage charging, electrochemically inactive Ni2+, Co2+, and Mn2+/3+ species become enriched at these contact regions, while oxygen depletion propagates inward across the particle surface. The LiNbO3 coating suppresses transition-metal reduction, improves surface electrochemical activity by increasing surface Ni and Co oxidation and confines oxygen depletion to the contact regions. Residual degradation nevertheless persists, consistent with inhomogeneous LiNbO3 coating coverage and its partial decomposition at high voltage. These findings provide nanoscale insight evidence that cathode and electrolyte degradation are interdependent and coupled through oxygen activity at the cathode surface and that effective coatings must suppress the cathode surface degradation.
