item.title: Metastable Olivine-Type Intermediates in Maricite NaFePO4 Cycling Revealed by Operando XRD and DFT
item.description: NaFePO4 (NFP) is a potential cathode material for sodium-ion batteries and exists mainly as the maricite and olivine polymorphs. Maricite NaFePO4 (m-NFP) is the thermodynamically stable and synthetically accessible polymorph of NaFePO4, with a theoretical capacity of 154 mAh g-1 but is expected to exhibit limited electrochemical activity due to the absence of continuous Na-ion migration channels in its crystal structure. Its reported electrochemical activity has been attributed either to amorphization or to crystalline reconstruction, and previous computational studies have modelled desodiation within the known maricite and olivine polymorphs separately. It has therefore remained unknown whether desodiation of m-NFP crosses polymorph boundaries, and if so, through which intermediate. Here, we combine operando X-ray diffraction (XRD) with density functional theory (DFT) calculations to resolve this pathway. Operando XRD shows that m-NFP retains its long-range crystallinity during cycling, while systematic peak shifts and new reflections reveal an at least partially reversible crystalline transformation. A common convex hull of maricite-, olivine- and alluaudite-type NaxFePO4 (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) identifies alluaudite-type Na0.67FePO4 as the thermodynamically preferred intermediate. Calculated voltages exclude a maricite-retaining pathway but cannot discriminate between the remaining candidates. Pathway-resolved simulated XRD fingerprints, however, show that the experimental peak evolution is most consistent with a metastable olivine-type intermediate, lying only about 8 meV/atom above the hull, rather than with alluaudite. Structural similarity analysis indicates that this intermediate retains a more maricite-like local environment, suggesting that structural accessibility, not thermodynamic stability alone, selects the pathway. These results reconcile conflicting reports on m-NFP and show that the electrochemically accessed pathway of polymorphic electrode materials need not follow the lowest-energy intermediate.

item.title: A generative neural network architecture for structure elucidation
item.description: Determining molecular structure is central to chemistry. One-dimensional (1D) 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a standard technique in small molecule structure determination, but deducing a structure from these spectra remains challenging because of the vast chemical space involved. Deep learning models that predict structures directly from NMR data have shown potential in navigating this space, but are trained largely on simulated spectra and perform poorly on real experimental data. Here we present a transformer model trained purely on experimental NMR data from approximately 1 million molecules, which takes 1D 1H and 13C NMR peak lists together with molecular weight (readily obtained from mass spectrometry) and generates candidate structures as SMILES strings. On a held-out test set, our model identified the correct structure among 15 candidates for 56.6% of molecules with up to 19 heavy atoms (34.8% overall). On a benchmark of 86 experimental spectra, it was more than four times as accurate as the published NMR2Struct model at every candidate pool size, while generating more chemically valid candidates. Even when the exact structure was missed, its best candidates remained structurally close to the target, and its incorrect candidates retained many of the target’s functional groups, making them useful starting points for structure elucidation. These results demonstrate that training on experimental spectra substantially improves structure prediction from routine 1D NMR data.

item.title: Selective Lanthanide-Binding Peptides: Molecular Insights into Binding Affinity and Selectivity
item.description: Rare earth elements (REEs), including the lanthanides, are essential to clean-energy technologies, semiconductors, electric vehicles, turbines, and other advanced materials that exploit their luminescent, magnetic, and catalytic properties. Current REE separation methods, however, suffer from poor selectivity, high solvent use, and environmental burden, which motivates greener and more selective strategies. Here we combine fluorescence binding measurements, molecular dynamics, enhanced-sampling calculations, descriptor analysis, and machine learning to determine how lanthanide-binding tag (LBT) peptides discriminate among trivalent REE cations in aqueous solution. The peptides operate in two binding regimes. For larger, lighter REEs, affinity is governed primarily by ion size, solvation, solvent accessibility, and non-bonded electrostatic interactions in a loosely coordinated binding pocket. For smaller, heavier REEs, the pocket contracts, and steric crowding, ligand–ligand electrostatic repulsion, and backbone torsional strain increasingly oppose further stabilization. Correlation analyses with sequence-derived, solvation, ligation, and conformational descriptors support this dichotomy. Analysis of selected LBT1-derived variants yields design rules: terminal charge tunes absolute affinity, ligating-residue geometry controls productive electrostatic coordination, a gatekeeper residue regulates water access and steric closure, and terminal residue hydrophobicity modulates amphiphilicity while preserving lanthanide-size sensitivity. Finally, classifiers trained on 37,041 sequences predict coarse Tb3+ affinity classes from a few bioinformatic descriptors, including disorder propensity, charge, amphiphilicity, and hydrophobicity, whereas predicting relative affinity across the full lanthanide series remains sensitive to solvation and binding-pocket remodeling. These results provide a molecular framework for engineering peptides for selective REE recovery and separation.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: Chiral Phonons Protected by Symmetry in a Strongly Anharmonic Helical Material
item.description: arXiv:2611.25089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How chiral phonons survive anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions, which underpin lattice dynamics at finite temperature, remains poorly understood. Using an ab initio many-body approach, we study crystalline tellurium (Te), a strongly anharmonic helical crystal. We show that rotational symmetries in Te impose pseudoangular momentum selection rules on phonon-phonon interactions, restricting mode mixing and scattering at rotationally invariant symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. These symmetries protect the circular polarization of vibrational modes at finite temperature but not their lifetimes such that the dynamic chirality of handed vibrational modes persists to 600 K, even as lifetimes drop sharply. We find that the temperature-dependence of angular momentum generated by a thermal gradient is governed by lifetimes rather than chirality, decreasing by two orders of magnitude between 10 and 600 K.

item.title: Machine Learning-Driven High-Throughput Screening of Equimolar and Non-Equimolar High-Entropy Carbides
item.description: arXiv:2611.25127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Search for optimal compositions among high-entropy ceramics are challenging due to large composition space, which are unable to test either experimentally or by \textit{ab initio} calculations. Here we present a high-throughput screening for equimolar and non-equimolar high-entropy carbides (HEC) among group IVB and VB transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb and Ta). Large Atomistic Model MACE, and deep learning based interatomic potential DeePMD trained on \textit{ab initio}-based dataset of structures are used to effectively screen over the thousands of potential non-equimolar compositions among high-entropy carbides of Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb and Ta transition metals. A set of both equimolar and non-equimolar HECs are predicted to be stable in order to further synthesize those compositions based on the predictions.

item.title: The phase diagram of fluid hydrogen near melting from machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on quantum Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2611.25178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissociation of molecular hydrogen increasing temperature or pressure may either occur gradually or abruptly, via a phase transition. Despite considerable experimental and theoretical efforts, the phase diagram of dense hydrogen at temperatures above solid melting is not precisely known. Here, we perform classical and quantum Path Integral molecular dynamics simulations of dense hydrogen using two machine-learned interatomic potentials both trained on quantum Monte Carlo energies and forces. The resulting phase diagram is constructed using state-of-the-art techniques. Both models show a first-order phase transition from the molecular to the atomic liquid terminating in critical points whose locations were determined using finite-size scaling techniques. Triple points, located at the highest temperature of the melting curve, are found at the intersection of the liquid-liquid lines with the melting curve and should lead to clear signatures in ramp compression experiments.

item.title: Learning Spin Hamiltonians from Interacting Magnon Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2611.25321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A neural network that learns an inverse map inherits the approximations of the forward solver used to generate its training data. We demonstrate this in the inference of spin Hamiltonians from synthetic neutron-scattering spectra and show how a fast many-body solver can overcome the limitation of linear spin-wave theory (LSWT). We consider a family of anisotropic triangular-lattice spin Hamiltonians at fields just above saturation, where magnon interactions shift and broaden the spectrum in ways that LSWT cannot capture. Using the truncated Hilbert-space ladder (THL) method, we compute the dynamical spin structure factor (DSSF) nonperturbatively within the one- and two-magnon space. THL is fast enough to generate large training sets of DSSF spectra, enabling us to train neural networks that accurately predict Hamiltonian parameters. By empirically benchmarking several neural-network architectures, we find that a one-dimensional convolutional network performs best. A learned forward decoder then reconstructs the DSSF from the predicted parameters, providing a rapid self-consistency check and a visualization of the predicted response. When interactions are strong, networks trained on LSWT and THL spectra infer markedly different parameters. Analysis of the Fisher information matrix shows that the measurement protocol, including which spin-correlation components are resolved and the momentum cut, determines which couplings can be identified. Combining machine learning with fast many- body theory is therefore essential for quantitative Hamiltonian inference from scattering data.

item.title: Weakly coordinating anions and solvents break the conductivity-transference-solvation tradeoff
item.description: arXiv:2611.25375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lithium-metal batteries promise high energy density, but common electrolytes trade ionic conductivity against the share of current carried by lithium ions and against how strongly solvent binds those ions. We show that simultaneously weakening both interactions of the lithium ion, with solvent and with anion, relaxes this trade-off. Thus, a weakly coordinating perfluorinated alkoxyaluminate salt in liquefied fluoromethane conducts 39.2 mS cm$^{-1}$ at 25 $^\circ$C while maintaining a lithium-ion transference number of 0.71. Molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that the anion prevents persistent ion aggregation and lowers the salt's dissociation penalty. Consistent with these properties, nickel-rich cathode/lithium-metal anode full cells charge at 10C at room temperature and at 2C at $-40$ $^\circ$C. We advance coordination strength as a design axis for future energy storage devices.

item.title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.25646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme). Here, we present AdsNet, an equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts adsorption energies in a single forward pass, which operates on a local graph restricted only to adsorbate atoms and its immediate surface neighbors within a cutoff radius. This local graph formulation decouples computational complexity from total system size while encoding continuous geometric features (interatomic distances and directional vectors) enabling sensitivity to subtle variations in local bonding environments. AdsNet adopts a message-passing architecture with scalar and vector node features over multiple interaction layers. Trained on AdsTraj, a dataset of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) calculated structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates (H*, C*, O*, CO*, OH*, HOCO*), the model achieves an adsorption energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces obtained via automatic differentiation enable structure relaxation through a projected gradient descent algorithm with adaptive line search, eliminating entire geometry optimizations. Additionally, AdsNet uniquely decomposes predicted adsorption energies into contributions from individual atoms within the local adsorbate graph - an interpretability feature unattainable with conventional machine-learning potentials. AdsNet thus establishes an accurate, highly efficient, and interpretable framework for large-scale adsorption energy prediction and local interface relaxation across various material surfaces.

item.title: momipy: A time-resolved momentum microscopy data analysis workflow
item.description: arXiv:2611.25888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photoemission momentum microscopy is an emerging approach to photoelectron spectroscopy that is transforming electronic band structure mapping at both laboratory-based and large-scale facilities. Its extension to time-resolved measurements has recently enabled major advances, ranging from the femtosecond imaging of exciton wavefunctions to dark-field photoelectron microscopy of light-induced dynamics and strong light-matter interactions. However, the rapid acquisition of high-dimensional data sets (including electron in-plane momenta $k_x$ and $k_y$, kinetic energy $E_\mathrm{kin}$, time $\Delta t$, and more) poses substantial challenges for data handling and analysis. A typical workflow encompasses data acquisition, exploratory visualization, calibration and targeted feature extraction, with data management ideally guided by FAIR principles. Here, we present momipy, a Python package that streamlines the momentum microscopy data analysis workflow efficiently and at low computational cost. Among other features, momipy provides interactive 4D data visualization, energy and momentum calibration, space-charge correction, and a broad selection of multidimensional data analysis routines, including binning, momentum-map extraction and time-, energy- and momentum-resolved model fitting. momipy is accompanied by a selection of interactive example scripts, supporting adoption of momipy by both experienced researchers and users new to momentum microscopy.

item.title: Thermal investigation of buffer and transition layers in AlGaN HEMT stacks
item.description: arXiv:2611.25928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate thermal transport in a set of thin-film layers used in modern HEMT designs. Our theoretical analysis employs three phonon-transport models of increasing sophistication, ranging from a relatively simple Debye-approximation model to a first-principles framework that incorporates Density Functional Theory (DFT)-derived harmonic and anharmonic phonon properties. To describe ternary semiconductors, alloy scattering is also considered, and to account for the properties of non-ideal, polycrystalline thin films, scattering at grain and film boundaries is taken into account. For modeling the specific samples at hand, the latter are fitted to thermal conductivity data measured with Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR). Overall, we find that the first-principles model performs best and produces the most physically consistent results. Special emphasis is placed on establishing a reliable procedure for determining intrinsic transport properties dominated by Umklapp scattering. Building on these, it is then possible to systematically add additional scattering terms to the models and assess how model-inherent factors, such as the treatment of scattering rates or the description of the phonon dispersion, affect model accuracy and overall predictive capabilities.

item.title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.26186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.

item.title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy: Roles of disordering and nanostructuring in electron and phonon transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.26213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work investigates how defect engineering and nanostructuring via severe plastic deformation influence electrical and thermal transport in the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi. High-pressure torsion (HPT) for up to N = 4 turns produces a hierarchical defect structure, including deformation twins at low strains, dislocations and Lomer-Cottrell locks at intermediate strains, and a high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries at large strains. While hardness naturally increases and saturates at ~520 Hv, both electrical and thermal conductivity exhibit an unusual increase upon HPT processing (from 0.953 MS m-1 and 10.3 W m-1 K-1 after homogenization to 1.003 +- 0.005 MS m-1 and 14.4 W m-1 K-1 after N = 4). Analysis based on the Wiedemann-Franz law indicates a modest increase in electron transport (~5%) and a significant increase in phonon transport (~100%) after HPT processing. The phonon mean free path remains small on the order of 0.6-1.1 nm, and comparison with the Cahill-Pohl model shows that heat transport occurs near the minimum thermal conductivity limit, where vibrational modes are strongly scattered. This suggests that the enhancement in thermal transport is not governed by conventional defect scattering, but it is hypothesized that modifications in atomic-scale disorder, such as deformation-induced short-range ordering, are responsible for this unusual behavior. Specific heat capacity increases after HPT, consistent with stored defect energy. The linear thermal expansion exhibits a non-monotonic behavior, decreasing initially due to internal stresses and relaxation effects, and increasing at higher strains due to grain boundary-induced anharmonicity. These findings highlight the complex interplay between defects, atomic-scale disorder, and nanostructure in governing the electrical and thermal properties of severely deformed high-entropy alloys via electron and phonon scattering.

item.title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.26533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials are trained on large, diverse DFT datasets, but their validation rests on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale molecular dynamics. Where no direct experimental validation is available, comparisons to physically motivated potentials are valuable for drawing insight. We distinguish static properties, which are thermally accessible, from emergent properties, which require work from an external fatigue stress to drive rare events, and compare the potentials on both. An EAM potential and the NequIP foundational potential both agree closely with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an anomalously low intrinsic stacking fault energy ($\sim7$ times lower than EAM) and thus predicts far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale flaw modeled after the classical Griffith crack problem. Per-atom energy distributions after loading show that the two potentials differ most at energies far above what is thermally accessible. We also document memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation as practical concerns for practitioners of these foundational model forms.

item.title: Theory of magneto-electrokinetics in unidirectional electrolyte flow: Hydrodynamic potential and Hall effect
item.description: arXiv:2611.26208v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for magneto-electrokinetic transport in dilute electrolytes under unidirectional flow and streaming current conditions. Unlike standard magnetohydrodynamics in liquid metals, where charge carriers are electrons and conductivity is typically uniform, electrolytes exhibit spatially varying ion densities and additional forces such as osmotic pressure. In steady state, the coupled Navier--Stokes, Nernst--Planck, and Poisson equations become analytically tractable. We derive a Boltzmann-like expression for ion distributions that incorporates both the electrostatic potential and a novel hydrodynamic potential arising from the magnetic field. This potential depends explicitly on the flow profile and is not screened close to the bounding walls. Applying the theory to Poiseuille flow, we derive expressions for the induced Hall potential and demonstrate its near-linear dependence on flow velocity and magnetic field strength, while remaining largely independent of salt concentration. To validate this one-dimensional framework, we analyze the two-dimensional spatial transients near the channel entrance. We demonstrate a separation of length scales: the Hall electric field and space charge adjust to the magnetic field almost instantaneously, whereas the macroscopic salt concentration wake develops over a much longer Graetz length dictated by the P\'eclet number. We also examine a similar flow with counterions only and no added salt, determining the resulting potential and ion distributions. This work offers new theoretical tools for understanding ion transport in microfluidic and electrochemical systems.

item.title: Strange metal at the Lifshitz transition
item.description: arXiv:2407.02270v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Strange metal behavior is widely observed in cuprates, ruthenates, and twisted bilayer graphene. We study quantum critical transport at a two-dimensional Lifshitz transition, where the Fermi surface hosts a van Hove singularity and changes from convex to concave. Self-consistently solving the fermion-boson coupled system, we demonstrate a linear-in-$1/\omega$ optical conductivity driven by the interplay between impurity and critical scattering. The resistivity exhibits a persistent linear-in-$T$ in the quantum critical regime down to $T\rightarrow 0$. Spatially fluctuating Yukawa interaction further extends the linear-in-$T$ regime, providing a unified mechanism for strange metallic transport at the Lifshitz transition.

item.title: Assessing the Transferability of General-Purpose MachineLearning Interatomic Potentials for Heterogeneous Catalysis with HetCat26
item.description: arXiv:2609.30621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise near-density functional theory (DFT) accuracy across broad areas of chemistry and materials science. However, their performance in describing systems and processes relevant to heterogeneous catalysis remains underexplored. Here, we introduce HetCat26, a collection of benchmark tests designed to assess pre-trained MLIPs across key aspects of catalytic modeling, including surface energetics, metal-metal oxide interactions, adsorption, and catalytic reaction networks. Evaluating eighteen foundation models, we find that performance on existing general materials benchmarks is only weakly predictive of performance on HetCat26; transferability to heterogeneous catalysis cannot be inferred from these general benchmarks. Across the benchmark tests, current models describe surface energetics and, perhaps surprisingly, reaction barriers well, whereas larger errors are observed for adsorption, and DFT site preferences are often not reproduced. Three models, eSEN-30M-OAM, SevenNet-Omni-i12 and MACE-MH-1-OMAT, nevertheless achieve high accuracy across the properties evaluated. Beyond model benchmarking, HetCat26 highlights the importance of training data consistency: PBE and PBE+U calculations should not be mixed within a training set. Overall, we identify challenges limiting the transferability of current foundation MLIPs to heterogeneous catalysis and, more broadly, to chemical reactions at interfaces, providing guidance for the development of the next generation of foundation models.

item.title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.18967v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $\nu = 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

item.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.00274v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $\mu$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

item.title: Physics-guided machine learning for sim-to-real calibration of NV diamond magnetometers
item.description: arXiv:2608.19582v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ensemble nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond enable robust magnetometry in unshielded environments, yet deployment remains bottlenecked by complex calibration and a reliance on external references. Conventional statistical machine learning requires massive training datasets and suffers from severe simulation-to-reality mismatches. To address this, we introduce a physics-guided hybrid machine learning framework that embeds Zeeman splitting directly into the learning pipeline. In an ablation study, our model demonstrates a nearly 3-fold improvement in precision and a 372-fold reduction in mean prediction bias over a purely statistical baseline. Furthermore, anchoring scalable synthetic data generation with just 49 sparse experimental seeds circumvents physical data scarcity while incorporating real-world non-idealities. Evaluated across a hybrid dataset of over 19,000 spectra spanning a 400 G dynamic range, the framework bridges the simulation-to-reality gap and achieves robust scalar field prediction, transferring effectively to raw, uncalibrated experimental data. Operating with minimal computational overhead on standard commercial hardware, the model achieves sub-4 ms inference times per spectrum, demonstrating strong viability for real-time edge deployment.

item.title: The Dichotomy Between Pattern Recognition and Step-by-Step Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.09186v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We argue that pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning are two ends of a spectrum. A large language model (LLM) learns to reason step-by-step when data is structured such that the next token depends on a small amount of preceding context. Inference in LLMs resembles pattern recognition when the next token depends on a large amount of preceding context. If the next token depends on only the $c$ most recent tokens, reasoning traces are paths on a de Bruijn graph whose nodes are $c$-length contexts and edges are next-token transitions between contexts. The set of reasoning traces of a task forms a directed acyclic subgraph of the de Bruijn graph. An LLM that has learned all edges of this subgraph can compose them to solve longer, unseen tasks, i.e., it reasons step-by-step. We prove that the number of edges is vanishingly small compared to the number of reasoning traces. We also prove and show empirically that the number of training samples a transformer needs is a linear in the number of edges, so learning to reason step-by-step is sample efficient. We can induce de Bruijn structure in any task by maintaining a ``state'' that makes future reasoning independent of the past. The frequency of states in the reasoning trace determines $c$. We show, by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to solve equations and answer questions about stories, that frequent states (small $c$) result in higher accuracy but greater fragility to perturbations at test time. LLMs trained with a large $c$ are only as good as models that perform pattern recognition without reasoning. A moderate density of states balances accuracy and robustness. Real-world data has de Bruijn structure: Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B retain over 75\% of their accuracy on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond when attention is restricted to a sliding window less than 15\% as long as the full reasoning trace.

item.title: ICPoly: An Automated Molecular Dynamics Workflow for Characterizing Structure, Dynamics, and Transport in Polymer Ion-Exchange Membranes
item.description: Predicting ionic transport in polymer ion-exchange membranes requires molecular models that connect polymer structure and hydration with local dynamics and collective charge transport. Here, we present ICPoly, an automated molecular dynamics workflow for characterizing the structure, dynamics, and ionic conductivity of these membranes. ICPoly integrates sequence-controlled polymer construction and fragment-based GAFF2 parameterization with staged classical and machine-learned equilibration, molecular-connectivity monitoring, and color-field nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD). Constant-field and constant-current formulations are implemented through modified Nosé–Hoover integrators in the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), while trajectory analysis characterizes the membrane structure and sulfonic acid deprotonation and predicts quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) spectra. The workflow is demonstrated for hydrated Nafion 212 in its proton and sodium forms using the reactive machine-learned UMA-s-1p2 potential. For representative Nafion-like fragments, UMA-s-1p2 achieves energy and force root-mean-square errors of 2.17 meV/atom and 41.84 meV/Å relative to density functional theory. The simulations reproduce the hydration-dependent decrease in density and reveal hydration-dependent changes in pore geometry and local organization, as well as incomplete sulfonic acid deprotonation. The two NEMD formulations yield similar velocity-based conductivity estimates. A displacement-based constant-field estimator shows faster apparent convergence but yields a substantially lower conductivity; it is adopted for subsequent calculations. Predicted proton and sodium conductivities increase with hydration, although proton conductivity is systematically underestimated and sodium conductivity is overestimated at low hydration. Overall, ICPoly provides a versatile and extensible computational framework that bridges polymer chemistry, molecular structure, dynamics, and ionic transport, enabling systematic investigations of structure–property relationships and facilitating the rational design of high-performance polymer materials.

item.title: GPU-accelerated analytic Hartree–Fock gradients
item.description: Analytic nuclear gradients play a central role in quantum chemistry, enabling geometry optimization, ab initio molecular dynamics, and the generation of reference data for machine-learned interatomic potentials. Despite substantial advances in GPU-accelerated self-consistent field (SCF) methods, implementations of the associated analytic gradients on GPU remain comparatively less developed, often requiring as much computational time as the preceding SCF. Here we present a novel, high-performance GPU implementation of the analytic Hartree-Fock energy gradient in EXESS. The Coulomb and exchange gradients are evaluated by separate engines to exploit their markedly different sparsity. The exchange gradient retains the full eightfold integral symmetry through an in-kernel ring-buffer compaction that eliminates warp divergence. A hybrid Head-Gordon-Pople/Rys quadrature scheme, translational invariance and GPU-resident shell-pair batch construction further accelerate the evaluation.We benchmark the implementation on NVIDIA H200 GPUs across double- and triple-ζ basis sets, on molecules of up to 11,577 basis functions (ubiquitin). EXESS is the fastest code for every system and basis set tested, with average speedups over TeraChem (12.2x), GPU4PySCF (15.4x), cuEST (24.5x direct, 13.3x Grid-K), QUICK (222x) and VeloxChem (176x).

item.title: MolScrub: an open-source tool to generate conformers and protonate drug-like molecules
item.description: We introduce MolScrub, an open-source Python-based tool to prepare drug-like molecules for structure-based simulations. MolScrub takes common molecular input specifications like SMILES, predicts the protonation states, and generates 3D structures. It is a high-throughput tool, having an average runtime of 0.3 to 0.5 seconds per molecule per CPU core. MolScrub returns as few protomers and conformers as reasonable to avoid feeding high-energy states to downstream simulations. Protonation state assignment includes both pKa prediction for acid-base pairs and tautomer enumeration. During 3D-coordinate generation, MolScrub enumerates 6-membered ring conformations to ensure that the final structure is close to a global minimum. These improved input geometries benefit docking programs that do not change the internal state of small rings. MolScrub was primarily developed to generate high-quality ligand structures to support docking-based virtual screenings but its modules (pKa prediction, tautomer enumeration, and ring geometry corrections) can be used and configured independently to support other applications.

item.title: Nanostructures strengthen titanium alloys
item.description:
Nature Materials, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41563-026-02801-5

Machine learning guides the design of an additively manufactured titanium alloy containing superfine features at the 10 nm scale through controlled martensitic transformation, which achieves an ultimate tensile strength of more than 1.7 GPa and 7.5% uniform elongation.

item.title: High-loading all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries enabled by tailored sulfur–sulfide and sulfur–carbon interfaces
item.description:
Nature Materials, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41563-026-02813-1

All-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries are a next-generation high-energy-density solution for energy storage. Here catholyte/cathode interfaces are found to be as important as transport tortuosity in thick sulfur cathodes, and an areal capacity of 10 mAh cm−2 is demonstrated at a stack pressure of 15 MPa and sulfur loading of 6.1 mg cm−2.

item.title: Linking human sources to antibiotic resistance genes in global surface waters
item.description:
Nature Communications, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79418-4

In this study, the authors used measurement data combined with modeling and machine learning to estimate global human generation of five individual ARGs and intI1, discharge, and surface-water abundance, highlighting hotspots of per-capita generation and total abundance.

item.title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of κ -Ga 2 O 3 thin films
item.description: The thermal conductivities of (001) κ-Ga2O3 thin films deposited on c-plane sapphire substrates were measured with frequency-domain thermoreflectance. The thermal conductivity increases from 1.83−0.18+0.19 to 2.26−0.40+0.35 W/m K as the thicknesses increase from 159 to 689 nm. This weak thickness dependence indicates that the majority of the intrinsic phonon mean free paths are smaller than the range of investigated film thicknesses. First-principles-based calculations that include phonon–phonon and phonon-boundary scattering capture this size-dependent behavior and support our experimental observation. Temperature-dependent measurements of a 689 nm film from 293 to 400 K show a decrease in thermal conductivity with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon–phonon scattering. A weaker temperature dependence is observed in a 159 nm film where phonon-boundary scattering becomes more prominent. At comparable film thicknesses, our measured κ-Ga2O3 films exhibit lower values of cross-plane thermal conductivity than the other experimentally measured Ga2O3 polymorphs. Our experimental observations are supported by prior predictions, which suggest that the low thermal conductivity of κ-Ga2O3 results from its complex crystal structure, which leads to increased anharmonicity and lower phonon group velocities relative to other polymorphs. Thermal management strategies, such as integration with high-thermal-conductivity substrates, may thus be required to mitigate self-heating for κ-Ga2O3-based electronic devices.

item.title: Long-range ionic mobility tuning under picosecond laser irradiation in KTiOPO 4 single crystals
item.description: Non-linear optical crystals often display a coexistence of ionic conductivity and bulk polarization at room temperature. We previously showed that the resulting ionic space charge increases drastically the Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) in KTiOPO4 (KTP) close to the crystal surface. We show here that laser irradiation in a plane is a way to induce and control such space charge at any depth in KTP single crystals. To this aim, we used a 1064 nm laser of average power less than 400 mW and with a repetition rate of 1 MHz leading to a pulse energy below 400 nJ. Thanks to the picosecond pulse regime providing spectral width in the GHz range, it covers efficiently the long-range ionic motion of K+ ions. By using a home-built XY scanning-SHG microscope, we designed specific incident laser trajectories to induce large-scale ionic gradients, thus increasing strongly the effective SHG signal, thanks to an additional Electric Field-Induced Second Harmonic contribution resulting from the generated ionic gradients. We suggest that the stabilized ionic space charge is triggered by the degenerated difference frequency process, called optical rectification, occurring in the GHz range. We anticipate such a result to be efficient in other non-linear optical crystals. In addition, our strategy is a low-cost alternative to the increasingly used high-power THz lasers.

item.title: Reconciling triple-phase boundaries and tortuosity in high-energy all-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries
item.description:
Publication date: 18 November 2026

Source: Joule, Volume 10, Issue 11

Author(s): Min-Gi Jeong, Michael Kindle, Yaobin Xu, Jie Bao, Jing Wu, Un-Hyuck Kim, Dahee Jin, Seunggoo Jun, Zhaoxin Yu, Hongliang Xu, Jun Liu, Jie Xiao, Dongping Lu

item.title: Towards a Metrological Validation of PFAS Property Predictions by In-Context LLMs Across Four Architectures
item.description: In recent years, the use of large-language models (LLMs) as prediction tools has become increasingly popular. Despite this popularity, the metrological validation of LLMs in the study of chemical problems has been somehow neglected to date. To illustrate this need in chemistry, we introduce a minimal, metrologically grounded framework for validating in-context learning (ICL)-based prediction in LLMs on molecular physicochemical properties with reliable estimation of uncertainty. Our framework integrates a multicycle testing protocol (Mc = 50 replicate cycles per model-property cell) with a six-metric bundle: central tendency (mean MAE over replicate cycles), reproducibility (interquartile range), regression performance (RMSE, and R2), information-theoretical lower bound on the amount of captured signal (𝐼" in nats), and ordinal 2 performance (accuracy against the median in the dataset), plus three cross-property and crossmodel comparison metrics: NRMSE, Welch’s z-test, and Scaling Law Fit exponents. We use this framework to validate four LLMs, two dense (8B and 70B parameters; 1B = 109) and two mixture-of-experts (MoE; 17B active parameters with 109B and 400B in total), for predicting eight per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) properties: boiling point (BP), melting point (MP), vapor pressure (VP), Henry’s law constant (HLC), octanol-water partition coefficient (LogKow), aqueous solubility (LogS), acid dissociation constant (pKa), and critical micelle concentration (LogCMC). In this benchmark, the frontier MoE model (Maverick 400B parameters) achieves a mean validation NRMSE of 14.4 %, and the mid-scale MoE model (Scout, 109B parameters) outperforms our larger dense model (Llama-3.3-70B) despite having 4.1× fewer active parameters. This suggests that MoE routed capacity can substitute for activeparameter scale in chemical applications of ICL. When compared to published QSPR and DFT baselines, LLM-ICL beats these approaches on three of eight directly comparable properties (pKa by 43 %, LogKow by 31 %, HLC by 10 %) and trails behind on five (BP, MP, LogS, VP by 12 % to 75 %, and LogCMC by a factor of approx. 3.3), despite using approximately 32 incontext examples (32 for seven properties, 20 for HLC) versus the training sets comprising 102 to 105 molecules used in these approaches. We also discuss a validation-set anomaly in the case of LogKow, where our mid-scale dense model Llama-3.3-70B outperforms the frontier MoE model on all four validation metrics, possibly due to better coverage of the pretraining data. Permutation (shuffled-label) and information-access blinding controls show that genuine structure-response signal is present, but that the native-prompt accuracy depends substantially on pretrained, property-specific knowledge and familiar target scales. Overall, our results suggest a two-fold conclusion on the competitiveness of LLM-ICL: it succeeds in predicting chemical

item.title: AMBER2LAMMPS: Validated conversion of AMBER-family topologies to LAMMPS
item.description: AMBER topology files encode a complete molecular-mechanics model rather than only molecular connectivity. Translating them to LAMMPS requires preservation of bonded parameters, charges, Lennard-Jones coefficients, exclusions, topology-specific 1–4 scaling, masses, and periodic-cell semantics. AMBER2LAMMPS is an open-source Python package that converts one or more fully parameterized AMBER topology templates and matching PDB coordinates to LAMMPS data and parameter files. The converter derives SCEE and SCNB scaling from active proper dihedrals, represents non-covalent GAFF2–GLYCAM mixtures with repeated hybrid pair-style instances, supports validated ff14SB, TIP3P, ion, and Li/Merz 12–6–4 cases, plus HMR mass mapping and TIP3P SHAKE initialization, and fails before output for unsupported combinations. Reproducible continuous-integration fixtures compare component energies and every Cartesian force against AmberTools sander. A command-line interface, Python API, and bounded Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface, with optional (CLI) or automatic (MCP) provenance, support both manual and automated workflows while keeping scientific decisions inspectable.

item.title: Informatics-Driven Chemputation within the HERA Framework: Mathematical Modeling of Molecular State Entropy, Reaction-Diffusion Flow Kinetics, and Closed-Loop Bayesian Optimization
item.description: The integration of physical chemical synthesis with digital information networks remains bottlenecked by the lack of unified frameworks for lossless molecular state serialization, secure long-range telemetry, and automated robotic re-materialization. This study introduces the HERA framework, a comprehensive model that converts chemical supply chains into executable digital information routing problems. We establish a rigorous information-theoretic foundation by defining total chemical state information entropy H(C) as a decomposition of structural discrete entropy (H_struct), thermodynamic vibrational entropy (H_vib), and compositional concentration entropy (H_conc). To bypass intractable high-scaling quantum mechanical calculations (O(N⁷) Coupled Cluster theory), we formulate Graph Neural Network (GNN) surrogate operators (H_GNN) that reduce computational complexity to O(N²) while bounding prediction error within ε_q <= 10⁷Hartree. Furthermore, we derive lossless HERA Data Container (HDC) compression bounds, reaction-diffusion transport kinetic partial differential equations governed by the Peclet number for continuous-flow Chemical Processing Units (ChemPUs), and Kullback-Leibler (D_KL) spectral divergence thresholds to enforce hardware safety and error-correction. Grounded in open analytical standards (mzML, nmrML, AnIML), chemoinformatics serialization (InChI, RInChI, xDL), and closed-loop Bayesian optimization within self-driving laboratories, HERA establishes a secure, dual-use protected pathway for decentralized pharmaceutical manufacturing, hazardous forensics, and deep-space astropharmacy.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: Counterions, polarization, and pore hydration relay drive ion permeation through hydrophobic pore formed by the MERS coronavirus E protein

item.title: Application of Pretrained Universal Machine Learning Force-Fields for Phase Transitions Prediction in ZrO2
item.description: arXiv:2611.23535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretrained universal machine-learning force fields can reduce the cost of finite-temperature molecular dynamics relative to density functional theory. However, most benchmarks test only static properties and do not assess whether these models reproduce the correct phase-transition sequence. Here, we benchmark ten open-source universal machine-learning force fields for zirconia (ZrO$_2$) using phonon dispersion calculations and variable-cell isothermal-isobaric molecular dynamics. Zirconia is a useful test because it has three thermodynamically stable crystalline phases prior to melting, following the sequence monoclinic-tetragonal-cubic. Four models reproduce this sequence: 7net-l3i5, MatterSim-v1.0.0-1M, MACE-mpa, and MACE-D3. Models with orthorhombic-tetragonal energy errors above about 10 meV/atom (7net-0, CHGNet, and MACE) instead produce an orthorhombic intermediate and predict monoclinic-orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic-liquid upon heating. ORB-based models fail to sustain stable variable-cell dynamics because their phonon frequencies are compressed by 30-60% relative to the density functional theory reference. Across all ten models, two ground-state diagnostics predict finite-temperature behavior. Relative polymorph energetics should agree with the matched density functional theory reference within about 6 meV/atom, and the phonon spectrum should not show systematic softening. These diagnostics are practical screening metrics for assessing pretrained force fields for phase-transition predictions.

item.title: Persistent Hydration and Ionic Mobility: When the Ion Is Not the Only Transported Species
item.description: arXiv:2611.23605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small-ion transport in water remains only partially understood despite more than a century of theoretical work. The difficulty is especially acute for strongly hydrated ions such as Li$^{+}$, Mg$^{2+}$, and Ca$^{2+}$, whose first hydration shells can persist on timescales comparable to or longer than translational motion. We develop a molecular framework in which the ion, its first hydration shell, and the outer solvent are treated as dynamically coupled components. Local hydration structure and exchange are represented through a potential of mean force and coordination dynamics, while collective solvent response is described through molecular memory functions. The theory clarifies why hydration cannot generally be represented by an additive friction or a single enlarged radius, and provides a route beyond conventional continuum and molecular descriptions.

item.title: Physics-Guided Crystal Structure Elucidation from Powder X-Ray Diffraction with Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.23760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.

item.title: Technical Note on Matlantis PFP v9: Extending the Element and Domain Coverage of the r2SCAN Training Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.23873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) make atomistic simulations possible at scales beyond the reach of density functional theory (DFT). Matlantis PFP is a uMLIP that treats a variety of domains, including crystals, molecules, and surfaces, with a single model. PFP v8 incorporated a training dataset computed with the r2SCAN functional, chosen for its good agreement with experiment, but the elements and domains covered by that dataset were limited. Here we present Matlantis PFP v9, in which the training data computed with the r2SCAN functional are extended to the lanthanides from Pr to Lu and to the elements from Po to Cm, for a total of 96 elements, and to additional domains such as clusters and adsorption structures. The formation energies of crystals containing the newly supported elements reproduce experimental standard enthalpies of formation with the same level of accuracy as crystals composed only of previously supported elements, and the adsorption energies of molecules on transition-metal surfaces have an overall error against experiment comparable to that of DFT-PBE, although chemisorbed species are overbound. On the same type of GPU (A100), the inference speed and the maximum system size exceed those of SevenNet-Omni, a public uMLIP trained on r2SCAN data: forces are evaluated three to four times faster, and five to ten times as many atoms can be handled. As a result, PFP-R2SCAN is now applicable to systems containing rare-earth and actinide elements and to adsorption on surfaces.

item.title: A GPU-Native Nested Sampling Framework for Finite-Temperature Materials Modelling with Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.24088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have dramatically improved the accuracy of and the scales accessible to atomistic simulation, yet the thermodynamic sampling methods needed to turn those potentials into finite-temperature phase stability predictions have not kept pace computationally. We present the GPU-native, massively parallel nested sampling framework JAXRENS, implemented on top of JAX, which removes the practical bottlenecks preventing atomistic nested sampling from being combined with state-of-the-art MLIPs. The framework provides distributed multi-GPU execution, vectorised ensembles of walkers, and direct interoperability with modern force fields. We demonstrate the highly beneficial scaling of JAXRENS on hardware accelerators, and apply it to the simulation of the ZnS phase diagram based on a MACE foundation model, a procedure previously computationally inaccessible. Despite requiring in the order of 10^10 model evaluations, the final converged simulation completed within six days on four GPUs, marking an important step towards routine, first-principles-quality predictions of finite-temperature phase stability using machine-learned interatomic potentials.

item.title: Machine learning interatomic potentials and orientational defects in polymers
item.description: arXiv:2611.24148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photopolymerization of acrylated epoxidized soybean oil (AESO) is a convenient model of a self-organizing process in a soft, bio-based material: ultraviolet light starts a free-radical chain reaction, the growing network releases heat, and the mobility of molecular groups changes on several time scales at once. We follow this process from two sides. Experimentally, the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity of an AESO:VDM (1:0.5) mixture with 3 mol% of the photoinitiator DMPA were recorded at 500-5000 Hz under an intermittent on/off illumination protocol, and the resulting time series were analysed with a sliding-window Shannon entropy and the Grassberger-Procaccia correlation integral. Both measures show that short light pulses at the start of curing trigger strongly correlated, collective relaxation, which fades as the network forms, leaving only localized reorientations active. We describe these reorientations as orientational defects and quantify their energetics with the MACE-OFF23 machine learning interatomic potential, using relaxed dihedral scans of five rotational modes ($\alpha$, $\alpha/\beta$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$) of an AESO fragment. Compared with density functional theory (DFT) reference profiles, MACE reproduces the shape of all five profiles (Pearson $r=0.95$-$0.98$) and the hierarchy of barriers - from 2.9 eV for the constrained main-chain rotation, through 0.54-0.81 eV for the acrylate rotations, to 0.16-0.18 eV for the methyl and 0.06 eV for the hydroxyl rotation - while underestimating the barrier heights by 3-20%. A simple Arrhenius estimate shows that the acrylate rotations are the modes closest to the frequency window of the dielectric measurement.

item.title: Characterizing adsorption thermodynamics in carbon capture materials: an efficient first-principles approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.24759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Porous materials offer a vast design space for CO$_2$ capture, whose exploration hinges on efficient and accurate first-principles predictions of the thermodynamics governing adsorption. However, simulating isotherms and heats of adsorption using grand canonical molecular simulations is extremely computationally expensive when combined with accurate ab initio treatments of the molecular interactions, limiting screening to low-pressure uptake encoded in the Henry constant. Identifying and designing the best CO$_2$ capture materials requires a strategy that can efficiently calculate their adsorption properties using ab initio potential energy surfaces such as those now available from foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Here we develop a neural classical density functional (cDFT) framework for carbon capture processes that allows direct calculation of adsorption isotherms from low to high loading limits of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) without grand canonical simulations. We demonstrate the success of our approach by calculating the ab initio adsorption isotherms for over 5,000 experimentally reported MOFs. From our screening, we show how these materials can be characterized using four isotherm shapes, arising from their pore size and binding sites, which the Henry constant cannot distinguish. We show that these shapes, rather than the binding strength alone, decide which MOFs suit which process: small pores with strong binding sites for vacuum and temperature swings at low pressure, large pores with weakly binding walls for pressure swings. Finally, we identify the most promising candidates by weighing their working capacity against the energy needed for regeneration.

item.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.23342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

item.title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description: arXiv:2611.23680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

item.title: XANES-Guided Molecular Structure Generation via Conditional Diffusion and Forward Spectral Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.23725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing complete molecular structures from X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra remains challenging because the spectra primarily encode local chemical environments, with overlapping contributions from multiple absorbing sites. Here, we develop an inverse-forward framework combining XANES-conditioned diffusion-based molecular structure generation with forward spectral prediction for candidate selection. The inverse model generates atomic species, bond connectivity, and three-dimensional coordinates from C, N, and O K-edge XANES, given only the total atom count without molecular formulas or element-specific atom counts. Combining all three absorption edges substantially improves structural recovery, achieving a best-of-10 exact-match rate of 56.6% across 2,888 test molecules. The generated candidates also reproduce functional groups and structural motifs, achieving a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.951 across 21 categories. Ranking candidates by agreement between input and forward-predicted spectra increases the exact-match rate from 24.3% for unranked top-1 selection to 43.9%. This spectral-consistency criterion also enables atom count estimation, identifying the correct count for 65.6% of molecules among seven tested values. Application to experimental spectra yields an exact structural match for imidazole and recovers characteristic functional groups in two additional molecules, while revealing limitations due to simulation-experiment spectral discrepancies. These findings establish an inverse-forward approach for reconstructing whole-molecule structures from complementary element-specific XANES information.

item.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.24013v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

item.title: UniMatSim: A High-Throughput Materials Simulation Automation Framework Based on Universal Machine Learning Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2603.15294v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (UMLIPs) offer accuracy close to first-principles calculations at a fraction of the cost, showing significant potential for large-scale material simulations. However, the fragmented UMLIPs ecosystem lacks unified interface standards and integration frameworks, hindering their automated deployment in high-throughput workflows. To address this, we present UniMatSim, a modular Python framework. It systematically integrates various UMLIPs (e.g., CHGNet, M3GNet, MACE) and automates workflows from structural optimization to stability verification. The framework enables seamless model switching via abstracted interfaces, incorporates task orchestration, and provides standardized modules for key properties (elasticity, phonons, molecular dynamics), including automated handling for low-dimensional materials. As a test case, using the 2D Lieb lattice system, we constructed a multi-stage high-throughput screening workflow covering structural optimization, elastic stability, and phonon spectrum calculations. Starting from 1,176 candidate compositions, a four-model consensus pipeline yields 393 stable structures. These are refined by magnetic-state screening and DFT band-structure calculations to 59 Lieb-lattice candidates with staggered-magnetic-band characteristics. Results show UniMatSim significantly improves computational efficiency and reproducibility, providing a reliable infrastructure for data-driven materials discovery and design.

item.title: Defect-limited thermal transport in AlN using pretrained machine-learning interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.08013v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aluminum nitride (AlN) is an important thermal management material whose high lattice thermal conductivity is strongly suppressed by oxygen impurities. We investigate phonon scattering by oxygen-related defects using pretrained universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), molecular dynamics (MD), and phonon Boltzmann transport calculations. Several pretrained MLIPs are benchmarked against density functional theory for phonon dispersions and pristine thermal conductivity. To balance accuracy and computational speed, we use a fine-tuned version of the compact SevenNet-Nano model for MD simulations. Monte Carlo annealing supports the formation of bound $V_{\mathrm{Al}}(\mathrm{O_N})_3$ complexes, whose scattering differs from that of their isolated constituents. Defect scattering rates extracted from excess spectral energy density (SED) linewidths agree reasonably with harmonic $T$-matrix predictions at low oxygen contents, supporting the independent-scatterer approximation. Incorporating these rates into an iterative Boltzmann transport equation with Bose--Einstein statistics yields thermal conductivities comparable to experimental values and captures their observed decrease with oxygen content. At high concentrations, however, the scattering rate deviates from linear scaling with oxygen content, suggesting limitations of independent-defect and pristine-phonon descriptions. These results demonstrate an efficient approach using pretrained MLIPs to quantify defect-limited thermal transport and provide insights into impurity effects beyond the dilute-defect approximation.

item.title: How anion composition governs structural frameworks and Li-ion transport in oxychloride solid-state electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2611.13611v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixed-anion lithium oxychlorides exhibit high Li conductivity, but the relationship between oxygen content, structural framework, and Li-ion transport remains unclear. Here, crystal structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials are used to examine $\mathrm{Li}_yM\mathrm{O}_x\mathrm{Cl}_{6-2x}$ ($M$ = Nb and Ta [Group 5] and $M$ = Ti, Zr, and Hf [Group 4]). Increasing oxygen content changes isolated chloride-rich polyhedra into one-dimensional chains and subsequently more highly connected two- and three-dimensional frameworks. In the Group 5 series, fast Li diffusion occurs over $x \approx 0.67$--1.5, where the Li sites form a three-dimensional percolating network. Potential of mean force maps and nudged elastic band calculations reveal that fast Li-ion transport requires a low-dimensional framework supporting long-range migration through undercoordinated Li sites with low barriers, together with similar energies across Li sites. Finally, we perform fine-grid compositional search, which identifies $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{0.67}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.67}$, $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{0.75}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.5}$, $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$, and $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$ as stable candidates with predicted room-temperature self-diffusivities of up to $\sim 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These findings establish how oxygen content controls framework and Li-ion transport, guiding the design of lithium oxyhalide electrolytes.

item.title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.22140v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.
