item.title: Optical birefringence in exfoliated non-van der Waals Na 2 Zn 2 TeO 6
item.description: The landscape of two-dimensional photonics has been dominated by van der Waals (vdW) materials. Expanding this library to include non-vdW layered systems promises enhanced environmental robustness and access to novel functionalities, such as strong ionic conductivity, yet their exfoliation remains challenging. Here, we establish Na2Zn2TeO6 (NZTO), a P2-type superionic conductor, as an exfoliable non-vdW optical material. We demonstrate that the highly disordered, mobile Na+ interlayer inherently facilitates mechanical cleavage down to few-nanometer thicknesses (about 4 nm). Optical interrogation via spectroscopic ellipsometry reveals NZTO as a wide-bandgap dielectric with pronounced optical birefringence (Δn ≈ 0.25) across the visible and near-infrared spectrum. The lattice dynamics, probed by temperature-resolved Raman spectroscopy, underscore the rigidity of the [Zn2TeO6]2− framework, which remains largely decoupled from the high ionic mobility. These results identify NZTO as a compelling platform for robust, anisotropic dielectric photonics, simultaneously opening a pathway toward the convergence of ionic transport and optical control, an emerging paradigm we term iono-photonics.

item.title: PSE-RepairBench: a simulator-grounded benchmark for evaluating large language model-based setpoint correction in executable chemical process flowsheets
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for applications in chemical process design support. However, a comprehensive evaluation platform for comparing the outputs of LLMs as to whether they function effectively on process simulators has not been sufficiently established. In this study, we constructed PSE-RepairBench, an execution-based benchmark targeting deviation correction in DWSIM flowsheets. We perturbed scalar parameters of existing unit operations in computable flowsheets. These parameters included temperature and pressure setpoints, reflux ratio, and feed stage. This procedure generated tasks in which the temperature, pressure, flow rate, or molar fraction of a specified component in a terminal output stream deviates from its base value. The LLMs were provided with the terminal output stream subject to evaluation and the target conditions, equipment settings, stream information, and simulator logs for these flowsheets with shifted setpoints, and were prompted to output a repair action specifying which setting values of which equipment should be corrected to which values. The generated repair actions were applied to the flowsheets, and the success of each repair was determined based on the recalculation results from headless execution. Evaluation of nine LLMs (GPT-based, Claude-based, and Gemini-based) showed repair success rates of 34–67%. Analysis of failure reasons, types of terminal output streams, and parameters targeted for repair revealed differences in LLM behavior and task difficulty. This study provides a foundation for evaluating the chemical process design support capabilities of LLMs based not on surface-level output or agreement with exemplars, but on actual simulator execution results.

item.title: Automated multimodal mining of structured data locked in the figures and tables of flow chemistry literature
item.description: Flow chemistry literature locks much of its quantitative process data inside figures and tables that show molecular structures as images, including the low-yield and failed reactions that machine learning most needs. Text mining cannot read these formats, and general-purpose vision-language models hallucinate plotted points and do not return the same answer twice. We present FlowFigTabMiner, an automated multimodal pipeline that mines this data into structured records by chaining five custom-trained YOLO models with chemistry-specific tools, a VLM text reader and an LLM adjudication step. On a benchmark of 30 figures and 30 tables it reaches an F1 of 0.874, against 0.848 for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.778 for Claude Sonnet 4.6. The advantage is clearest on figures. Applied to organolithium flow chemistry, the mined data enabled a kinetic model whose yield predictions were tested on two substrates outside the corpus. Pipeline and dataset are open-sourced.

item.title: High Li+ Transference Number of a Novel Fluorine-Free Lithium Salt in Carbonate Electrolyte: DFT and Molecular Dynamics Insights into Dilithium 2,5-Dioxopiperazine-1,4-Disulfonate (LiDPSO)
item.description: Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly constrained by the drawbacks of fluorinecontaining commercial lithium salts, including hydrolysis hazards and the environmental burden of fluorinated species. Developing fluorine-free lithium salts with a high Li+ transference number tLi may offer a route to avoid fluoride-derived hazards, mitigate concentration polarization, and potentially lower lithium dendrite risks in applicable cell systems. Inspired by the zwitterion shielding effect, this work proposes an intramolecular likecharge shielding (ILCS) conceptual model and computationally examines a novel fluorine-free salt, dilithium 2,5-dioxopiperazine-1,4-disulfonate (LiDPSO), in EC/DMC carbonate electrolytes using density functional theory (DFT) and large-scale all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. DFT cluster–continuum and nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations reveal that the covalently anchored dual sulfonate sites provide intramolecular like-charge shielding that facilitates dissociation of the first Li+, whereas dissociation of the second Li+ is energetically unfavorable, favoring the contact ion pair [LiA]-. Continued solvation of [LiA]- enlarges its hydrodynamic radius and suppresses anion diffusion, which is expected to raise tLi. Backbone carbonyl groups build an intramolecular solvation microenvironment, enabling low-barrier Li+ hopping between the two sulfonate sites in [LiA]-. In MD simulations (>105 atoms systems), benefiting from combined vehicular transport, intramolecular hopping and Grotthuss-like Li+ exchange, the system achieves a high simulated tLi of ~0.73–0.74, versus ~0.41 for LiPF6, while retaining a Li+ conductivity comparable to that of LiPF6. Absolute simulated values may deviate from experiment, yet relative trends are often reproducible. If future experiments confirm both a high tLi and an acceptable Li+ conductivity for LiDPSO, this compound would be a promising fluorine-free lithium salt candidate, and the ILCS conceptual model, associated intramolecular coordination and symmetric dual-site motifs could offer new design guidelines for other innovative lithium salt anions.

item.title: AIMETRY: GEOMETRY-SENSITIVE 3D MOLECULAR REPRESENTATIONS FROM QUANTUM MECHANICAL LEARNED FEATURES
item.description: Quantifying molecular similarity depends on both chemical composition and 3D structure, which are difficult to capture in a single fixed-length representation. Contrastive learning is a common machine learning approach to generate such representations (molecular embeddings), pulling each molecule toward a positive anchor of itself. These anchors typically come from graph augmentations that alter chemical identity or from other conformers of the same molecule. However, using conformers as positive anchors in standard contrastive learning suppresses geometric distinctions and graded structural relationships. Here, we introduce AIMetry, a geometry-sensitive representation learning scheme in which a graph transformer aggregates spatially and chemically aware atomic features from AIMNet2, a machine-learned interatomic potential trained on quantum-chemical data, into a molecular embedding. We guide standard contrastive learning using fingerprint similarity, which modulates embedding similarity between different-molecule pairs, and root-mean-square deviation, which modulates embedding similarity between conformer pairs. Trained on approximately 44 million conformers of 2.8 million ChEMBL molecules, AIMetry demonstrates higher retention of fingerprint-defined structural relationships and greater geometric sensitivity than a reference model pretrained with standard contrastive learning. AIMetry also improves linear-probe performance relative to the reference model across the evaluated datasets, while benefits under nonlinear readout and fine-tuning are task-specific. Chemical and conformational analyses provide complementary evidence about the information retained in the representation.

item.title: N-Alkyl Cyanopyridinium Salts as Modular N-Terminal Cysteine Warheads for Site-Specific Bioconjugation and Living Cell Engineering
item.description: Site-specific protein modification is central to chemical biology and to therapeutic development. Stringent control over a single site delivers homogeneous conjugates and underpins the synthetic engineering of proteins and cells, which demands streamlined and reliable chemistry. An N-terminal cysteine (NCys) represents a unique canonical amino acid handle easily incorporated into peptides, proteins, and cells, yet its use remains underexplored. Building on 2-cyanobenzothiazole (CBT), we show that quaternizing the ring nitrogen of an otherwise sluggish cyanopyridine gives N-alkyl 4-cyanopyridinium salts (4CP+) with markedly improved kinetics, aqueous solubility, synthetic accessibility, and modularity. Moreover, 4CP+ reacts selectively with NCys to deliver a wide range of biochemical reporters and tumor-receptor ligands to peptides and proteins, enabling modular assembly of functional conjugates, as exemplified by smallmolecule–protein hybrid T cell engagers. We further developed a divinyl 4CP+ that rebridges native disulfides while retaining the nitrile as a latent handle for late-stage payload installation, extending NCys chemistry to modular synthesis of homogeneous therapeutic conjugates from cyclic peptides to off-theshelf monoclonal antibodies. We also demonstrated that a genetically encoded NCys serves as a minimal conjugation tag, which, paired with 4CP+ reagents, achieves site-specific protein labeling on live cell surfaces, including a natural killer cell line, opening up cell-conjugation applications.

item.title: Cross-Facility Materials Discovery Platform: Integrating Heterogeneous Data and Automated Experimental Pipelines into High-Throughput Workflows
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven materials discovery depends on the availability of large, highly annotated experimental datasets. However, data generated in typical materials science projects are fragmented across heterogeneous instruments, laboratories, and user facilities, each with its own formats, schedules, and degree of curation. In addition, manual sample preparation, time-consuming characterization, and changing sample form factors and holders between process steps often limit throughput and therefore dataset size. Here, we present a modular cross-facility workflow that addresses both the physical and the data bottlenecks. We combine robotic thin-film deposition, a custom robotic UV-vis setup, and high-throughput synchrotron end stations with custom, QR-code-tagged sample holders, preserving each film’s identity as it moves between experimental setups. Using Crucible, a schema-free data management platform developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, we link every sample, container, and dataset into a provenance network that traces each thin film through synthesis, deposition, characterization, and analysis. A Python client and custom web interfaces connect the Molecular Foundry with two beamlines at the Advanced Light Source and enable streamlined, high-throughput data collection pipelines. To demonstrate this workflow, we fabricated 6,105 thin films spanning 618 hybrid metal halide compounds over six months, of which approximately 3,400 were characterized by robotic grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering and 2,000 by residual gas analysis under extreme-ultraviolet exposure, generating a highly curated AI-ready materials discovery dataset that accurately reproduces a subset of matched manually prepared samples. We further demonstrate automated downstream analysis, including human-in-the-loop machine-learning classification and mechanistic evaluation of structure-property relationships. Together, the dataset and infrastructure provide a blueprint for scaling materials experimentation to facility-level AI platforms.

item.title: FLAMES – A flexible and extensible code for Monte Carlo simulations of nanoporous materials
item.description: Molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations are the cornerstone for computational studies of adsorption in nanoporous materials such as zeolites, Metal-Organic Frameworks, and Covalent Organic Frameworks. Currently, most of these simulations rely on classical force fields, which are often limited in their ability to describe specific interactions or the intrinsic flexibility of the host framework. Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a powerful alternative, offering near ab initio accuracy while remaining computationally feasible, potentially capturing framework flexibility and complex potential energy surfaces. Despite this promise, there is a significant gap, as current tools implementing MLIPs are often general-purpose codes adapted for adsorption or in-house solutions. Here, we introduce FLAMES (Flexible Lattice Adsorption by Monte Carlo Engine Simulation), a new software package designed to perform Monte Carlo-based simulations of nanoporous materials using MLIPs and other energy calculation methods, paving the way for more accurate and physically realistic molecular simulations. We detailed the implementation of different methodologies, including Widom insertion, Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC), hybrid GCMC/MD, and Transition Matrix Monte Carlo simulations, presenting validation examples for each method and evaluating the performance and accuracy of different energy calculation methodologies.

item.title: Reaction‐Programmed Dual‐State Molecular Engineering Decouples Mechanical Reinforcement and Ion Transport for Durable Flexible Zinc Devices
item.description: Advanced Energy Materials, EarlyView.

item.title: Dynamics and transport in LiF using classical and machine learned interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.21900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We perform molecular dynamics simulations of molten Lithium Fluoride, comparing the classical Buckingham and Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials with machine-learnt interatomic potentials - the MACE-MP-0b3 (small) foundation model potential, and a fine-tuned version thereof. We find that the MACE-MP-0b3, out-of-the-box, is able to accurately reproduce the experimental shear viscosity across the liquid state comparable with polarisable potentials despite not itself being polarisable. Previous viscosities computed using classical potentials are under-predicted, which has previously been attributed to a suppressed melting temperature. Prompted by this we compare the melting points of these potentials. We find that the machine-learnt potentials address the significant underestimation of the melting point of the classical potentials, though the refined potential and the foundation model differ significantly between themselves. We probe the microscopic structure and dynamics of each model to further elucidate the considerable change in viscosity between classical and machine-learnt potentials. We find that, despite their lower melting temperature, classical potentials produce considerably stiffer, higher frequency, single-particle and collective charge-transport dynamics on account of their fixed charges. However, in the long-wavelength limit, the many-body machine-learnt potentials feature more elastic collective motion that governs the diffusion of momentum and is therefore responsible for the enhanced shear viscosity.

item.title: quantEM: Quantitative Electron Microscopy Analysis from Differentiable Physics to Neural Priors
item.description: arXiv:2611.21903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantitative electron microscopy includes imaging, diffraction, spectroscopy, and tomography measurements, and the analysis of these measurements increasingly requires solving inverse problems with physical forward models. Open-source software has made many of these analyses widely available, but most packages are organized around a single modality, so that multimodal analyses require moving data between packages, and new methods cannot easily reuse the physical models and optimizers of existing ones. Here we present quantEM, an open-source Python package for quantitative electron microscopy that uses PyTorch tensors for computation and automatic differentiation, and Zarr for storage. We implement each analysis method by writing a differentiable forward model and choosing a representation, loss function, constraints, and optimizer from a library of components, so that every method runs on CPUs and GPUs, can be saved and resumed, and uses the same calibrated data structures and visualization tools. We describe the current modules, including orientation and strain mapping, direct and iterative ptychography, tomography with neural representations, and X-ray and electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and show how we assemble combined methods such as ptychographic tomography from existing components. quantEM is available under the MIT license, together with documentation, tutorials, and curated example datasets.

item.title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.22444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

item.title: First-order correction to the self-consistent harmonic approximation free energy: Impact on the negative thermal expansion and phonon dynamics in ScF$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2611.22538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strongly anharmonic crystals are often treated using the self-consistent harmonic approximation with variationally optimized Gaussian density matrices or the related self-consistent phonon theory. Both approaches capture substantial phonon renormalization but exclude connected non-Gaussian free-energy correlations. Here, we derive the first-order post-variational correction generated by the lowest non-vanishing normal-ordered residual vertex. Normal ordering the residual interaction around the optimized state shows that the linear and quadratic vertices vanish at the stationary variational solution, leaving a fluctuation-dressed cubic interaction whose second-order vacuum and two-point contractions generate the free-energy correction and the dynamical bubble self-energy, respectively. In ScF$_3$, the variational optimization on the full Born-Oppenheimer potential accounts for most of the shift in the thermal-expansion crossover temperature between negative and positive values relative to self-consistent phonon theory with a fourth-order potential. The connected correction changes the crossover modestly, but its volume derivative appreciably shifts the pressure-remapped cubic local-stability limit. Using the bare cubic vertex appears to improve agreement with the thermodynamic measurements, yet it systematically underestimates the measured zone-boundary tilt-mode energies at high temperatures. The fluctuation-dressed interaction gives more moderate thermodynamic corrections but yields phonon energies in better agreement with experiments. These results show that connected non-Gaussian correlations can significantly affect free-energy derivatives and soft-mode dynamics near a structural instability, and identify the optimized Gaussian state as the natural reference for constructing residual interactions beyond the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation.

item.title: Prior-guided adaptive local refinement of foundation interatomic potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.22626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation interatomic potentials enable simulations across diverse materials, but task-specific inaccuracies can require additional first-principles data. Obtaining these data is challenging when the relevant local environments arise in large simulation cells. Here we introduce the Prior-guided Adaptive Refinement Scheme (PARS), which identifies weakly supported environments during molecular dynamics by comparing their frozen representations with prototypes of pretraining environments, without requiring initial task labels or model ensembles. Selected environments are reconstructed as compact periodic cells for first-principles labelling and iterative refinement. Applications to phase stability, surface migration and vacancy clustering show improvements in target properties, including an 81% reduction in the mean absolute error of Ti vacancy-cluster energies per vacancy relative to the pretrained model. For Si/Ge, a foundation potential refined using 800 labelled cells containing 10-128 atoms is subsequently distilled into a compact potential without additional first-principles training labels. In simulations containing approximately 362,880 atoms, the distilled model predicts an interfacial thermal resistance consistent with that of a potential trained directly on density-functional theory data. These results demonstrate a route for adapting foundation potentials to target applications through local reference calculations.

item.title: VQkit: A Unified and Extensible Framework for VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO Pre- and Post-Processing
item.description: arXiv:2611.22664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: VQkit is a Python-based computational toolkit developed to streamline the pre- and post-processing of density functional theory calculations performed using Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) and Quantum ESPRESSO (QE). The framework employs a unified representation of lattice vectors, atomic coordinates, chemical species, and positional constraints, enabling cross-code structure conversion, geometry manipulation, crystallographic reconstruction, and code-specific input generation. Its pre-processing capabilities include symmetry-dependent reciprocal-space path generation, atomic constraints, and automated preparation of simulation inputs. The post-processing framework provides calculation convergence inspection, extraction of total energies and Fermi levels, electronic band-structure and density-of-states analysis, orbital-resolved electronic-structure processing, charge-density analysis, and evaluation of application-specific materials properties. The computational implementation is evaluated through elastic-property benchmarks for HfC, ZrC, ZrO2, Ti, and diamond, showing close agreement between VQkit and VASPKIT for VASP-based calculations, with differences observed in the corresponding QE results. By integrating cross-code interoperability, automated simulation preparation, standardized post-processing, and quantitative property evaluation within a common computational environment, VQkit reduces workflow fragmentation and facilitates consistent pre- and post-processing of first-principles calculations.

item.title: Universal scaling of brine migration in ice
item.description: arXiv:2611.22765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sea ice hosts mobile brine inclusions whose migration influences salt redistribution, microstructure and transport within the ice. Although their motion under temperature gradient is commonly described as a diffusion-limited process, experimental evidence has remained rare and insufficient because migration is slow and controlled inclusion seeding is challenging. Here we introduce an experimental method to trap and monitor hundreds of inclusions in ice under controlled temperature gradients. Using four solutes, three imposed gradients and two order of magnitude in initial concentration, we quantify migration dynamics over a broad range of conditions. We find that, except close to the ice front, inclusion migration is consistent with a regime limited by solute diffusion. After applying a universal scaling, both our data and previous measurements collapse onto a master curve, providing a general framework for describing solute transport in ice.

item.title: Emergent Attraction and Competing Orders near the Van Hove Singularity in Rhombohedral $n$-layer Graphene
item.description: arXiv:2611.23232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral $n$-layer graphene exhibits a rich phase diagram with multiple distinct superconducting regions, whose microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we investigate the competition between charge-density-wave (CDW) and pair-density-wave (PDW) instabilities near the inner van Hove singularities (VHSs), using a patch renormalization-group approach with the realistic band structures incorporated. We identify two key findings. First, we find an effective attractive interaction emerging from purely repulsive interactions through RG flow in the presence of $C_3$ symmetry breaking. The resulting interaction structure, with two repulsive couplings and one attractive coupling, gives rise to competing CDW and PDW instabilities. Second, the competition is controlled by the detuning from the VHS. While CDW dominates near the VHS filling and at higher temperatures, PDW becomes the leading instability on either side of the VHS and at lower temperatures. This mechanism naturally produces two superconducting regions separated by a CDW-dominated regime, providing a possible qualitative explanation for the experimentally observed separation between SC1 and SC2.

item.title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
item.description: arXiv:2611.22050v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

item.title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.22140v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.

item.title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
item.description: arXiv:2611.22623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman \rho = 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

item.title: An open dataset of gas adsorption in deformable metal-organic frameworks for direct air capture
item.description: arXiv:2508.03162v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Engineering economical and scalable processes for direct air capture (DAC) from humid air relies on atomistic modeling to search and identify promising sorbent materials from a vast chemical space. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for predicting material properties in an efficient yet accurate manner, but these models require large sets of carefully curated training data. We present the Open DAC 2025 (ODAC25) dataset comprising nearly 60 million DFT single-point calculations for CO2, H2O, N2, and O2 adsorption in ~15,000 MOFs. ODAC25 introduces functionalized MOFs, high-energy adsorbate placements, and synthetically generated frameworks to maximize the versatility of models trained on the dataset. ODAC25 improves upon the accuracy of DFT calculations in previous works and applies engineering intuition from recent work regarding the treatment of adsorbate-induced MOF flexibility. We release state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on ODAC25 and demonstrate their utility via Henry's coefficient predictions. ODAC25 enables MOF screening for DAC at a resolution previously unattainable.

item.title: Theory of Melting Lines with Variable Enthalpy of Fusion: Independent Verification of Phonon Theory of Liquids - Predicted Parabolic Behavior
item.description: arXiv:2605.17631v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To address the complex thermodynamics of the solid-liquid transition, we develop an analytical model by modifying the Clausius-Clapeyron (CC) equation to account for a variable enthalpy of fusion along the melting line (ML). This model draws upon theoretical and experimental progress demonstrating that the ratio of isobaric heat capacity to the thermal volume expansion coefficient in the solid state is a material constant that correlates directly with the fusion enthalpy and coexisting phase specific volumes. Differentiation of this modified CC relation yields a second order differential equation governing the low-pressure melting curve. By imposing appropriate physical boundary conditions, physically acceptable approximate parabolic solutions are derived. Rooted in solid-state lattice anharmonicity and variable fusion enthalpy, this work provides an independent theoretical derivation for the universal parabolic behavior of low-pressure melting curves. By complementing recent formulations from the Phonon Theory of Liquids [Trachenko, Phys. Rev. E 109, 034122 (2024)], this framework helps establish a dual theoretical foundation for solid-liquid phase boundary thermodynamics.

item.title: Adiabatic preparation of a fractional quantum Hall fluid by coherently pumping atoms from a Bose-Einstein condensate
item.description: arXiv:2606.15951v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a protocol to adiabatically prepare a many-particle fractional quantum Hall fluid of bosonic ultracold atoms exploiting a time-dependent coherent coupling of a strongly interacting atomic state with a large dilute Bose-Einstein condensate. Starting from an empty cloud, atoms with well-defined angular momentum are coherently pumped into the fluid by Raman beams with a Laguerre-Gauss profile. Compared to number-conserving schemes which rely on finite-size-induced gaps, we identify an adiabatic path in the Fock space which avoids crossing fixed-particle-number phase transitions and maintains a sizable and externally controlled adiabatic gap open at all times. The efficiency of our preparation protocol is numerically assessed for typical experimental parameters up to particle numbers that largely exceed the experimental state-of-the-art. The crucial advantage of including an anharmonic confinement is finally highlighted.

item.title: Functional Compression as Occam's Razor: Algebraic Complexity from Sensitivity Minimization
item.description: arXiv:2511.23152v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Discovering discrete algebraic structures from data is a fundamental challenge in machine learning. We ask how continuous learning objectives can favor functional compression---representing data through shared algebraic composition rather than low-rank representations. We analyze the global optima of a canonical factorization model for algebraic completion (recovering finite binary operations) that demonstrated a preference for group operations. We measure algebraic complexity by the infimum of parameter sensitivity under exact reconstruction. We establish a universal complexity floor, whose attainment forces geometric alignment and unitarity of the latent representations. At the floor, input representations compose into the corresponding output representations; their reuse across the operation table propagates these local identities to enforce a globally shared algebraic structure. If the floor is not attained, a positive gap separates it from the feasible infimum. For cancellative operations, floor attainment forces the model's latent representation to be an injective homomorphism, equivalent to the target being isotopic to a group. In this case, every global minimizer is equivalent to the underlying group's unitary left-regular representation, up to isotopy and unitary gauge, resolving the central conjecture of Huh (2025). For non-cancellative operations, floor attainment forces exact structural redundancies (identical rows or columns) and is equivalent to a unitary factorization of the target's row- and column-reduced table with orthonormal output matrices, yielding the fewest distinct input matrices compatible with exact reconstruction. The resulting cancellative table then embeds in a group-isotope table. This analysis reveals a structural bias toward functional compression: at the sensitivity floor, algebraic composition of latent representations implements the target operation.

item.title: A closed-loop framework for perovskite precursor additive discovery
item.description: arXiv:2605.20242v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient discovery of precursor additives is essential for improving the performance of perovskite solar cells, yet the large chemical space makes conventional trial-and-error screening inefficient. Here we show that LEAP (LLM-driven Exploration via Active Learning for Perovskites), a closed-loop framework combining a domain-specialized language model with active learning, prioritizes perovskite precursor additives under low-data conditions. The model extracts mechanism-relevant knowledge from the literature and converts it into interpretable molecular descriptors for uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimization. On an evaluation drawn from unseen literature, the specialized model provides more mechanism-consistent answers than the tested general-purpose models. In an expert-guided proof-of-concept study, two later-round additives increase average device power conversion efficiencies to 20.13% and 20.87%, compared with 19.25% for the control, and the best device reaches 21.32%. Because only a limited number of candidates are tested prospectively, these results provide preliminary evidence that literature-grounded molecular representations, Bayesian optimization, and expert assessment can support additive discovery for perovskite solar cells.

item.title: MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research
item.description: arXiv:2610.34203v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Materials research relies on scattered and growing data, knowledge, and simulation tools, and a single study often spans multi-day workflows across literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with new capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost-score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, it outperforms Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. Code is available at https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS.

item.title: Using potential derivatives to reduce the cost of rectangular collocation: a general and versatile approach for computational vibrational spectroscopy without a potential energy surface
item.description: We modify the exact Cartesian kinetic energy operator, rectangular collocation approach of Manzhos and Carrington [J. Chem. Phys. 145 (2016) 224110] by using information contained in potential derivatives to decrease the number of required potential points. We show that this makes it possible to substantially reduce the number of collocation points, which is important, in particular, when energies are computed directly ab initio. Vibrational band intensities are also computed. We first demonstrate the method on Cl2CO and compare to high-accuracy Smolyak collocation calculations on an accurate potential energy surface (PES). Sub-cm-1 accuracy is obtained with a few thousand Gaussian basis functions and potential points. A spectrum computed directly from DFT energies and a comparison to GVPT2 (generalized vibrational perturbation theory) are also presented. We then consider LiCO2 as a more anharmonic case, for which a quartic force field potential is less reliable, and which also serves as a surrogate model for a catalytic system (mimicking CO2 bond weakening by charge donation). The rectangular collocation method is used to compute the spectrum of LiCO2 directly from ab initio energies and to compare to GVPT2. The method is implemented as a Claude Skill and is easily usable by anyone on any molecule. The method is a general and versatile tool for anharmonic computational vibrational spectroscopy. It does not require a PES and no coupling is neglected.

Initially anode-free all-solid-state batteries with Ag-C interlayers promise high energy density but degrade in the cold. Here, authors identify suppressed Li-Ag alloying as the failure mechanism and introduce an activation protocol enabling durable cold cycling of pouch cells without material redesign.

item.title: Axially threaded nanoreactors synchronizing ion migration and electron replenishment for high-performance zinc–iodine batteries
item.description: Aqueous zinc–iodine batteries have attracted considerable attention owing to their high safety and fast iodine redox kinetics. However, soluble polyiodide shuttling, interfacial passivation, and insufficient charge replenishment severely limit their rate capability and cycling lifespan. Herein, an asymmetric Ni–N3 single-atom nanoreactor was constructed and serially embedded into carbon nanofibers, forming an axially continuous cowpea-like architecture. Benefiting from spatial confinement and polarized Ni–N3 sites, this architecture strengthens polyiodide adsorption, regulates interfacial charge distribution, and lowers the energy barrier for I2/I− conversion. Meanwhile, the carbon nanofiber backbone establishes an efficient electron-transport pathway, enabling the synchronous coupling of ion migration, interfacial catalysis, and charge replenishment, thereby effectively suppressing polyiodide shuttling, self-discharge, and interfacial passivation. The resulting electrode maintains an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.60% over the final 1000 cycles of 80 000 cycles at 20 C, providing an effective strategy for addressing the shuttle effect and kinetic limitations in zinc–iodine batteries.

item.title: Li 5 SmSi 4 O 12 : An inorganic lithium solid-state electrolyte enabled by ion exchange
item.description: Solid-state batteries (SSBs), which replace organic liquid electrolytes with solid counterparts, have attracted considerable attention for their enhanced energy density and safety. As a key SSB component, inorganic superionic lithium conductors have been discovered in only a few material classes, mostly via direct synthesis. Among these, silicate sodium superionic conductors of the type Na5LnSi4O12 (Ln = rare earth elements) offer stable anionic frameworks and favorable ion-transport channels. In this work, we reveal a rhombohedral superionic lithium conductor, Li5SmSi4O12, synthesized by ion exchange between LiTFSI and the sodium superionic conductor Na5SmSi4O12. Na+ ions are effectively replaced by Li+ ions while preserving the isostructure. Specifically, composite electrolytes with the ionic liquid EmimTFSI and with halide‐based Li2ZrCl6 exhibit ionic conductivities of 1.79 × 10−3 and 4.83 × 10−4 S cm−1 at 25 °C, respectively. Reversible charge−discharge cycling of lithium metal batteries is demonstrated using these Li5SmSi4O12 composite electrolytes and Li5SmSi4O12-modified separator. Our work unlocks the potential for creating inorganic lithium superionic conductors within a prototypical, chemically flexible structure, paving the way toward new solid‐state electrolytes.

item.title: MeCoBi: Fast and accurate 3D metal complex structures for structure-based machine learning
item.description: The three-dimensional arrangement of ligands around a metal centre determines its electronic structure, reactivity, and biological activity, yet generating accurate 3D structures from a string-based input remains difficult. Existing tools are slow, narrow in coverage, or need the coordination environment to be specified by hand. We present MeCoBi (Metal Complex Builder), an automated pipeline that builds and optimises 3D structures of mononuclear metal complexes from ligand SMILES across 36 d-block and main-group metals and coordination numbers 2–9. On 30,830 experimental structures from the Cambridge Structural Database, MeCoBi generated a structure for 99.6% of complexes with a median error in metal–ligand bond lengths of 0.06 Å. Used as machine-learning inputs, these structures ranked the untested members of an in-house library of 1,800 iridium complexes at least as well as the best 2D models (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.88 against at most 0.86); and, through GFN2-xTB single points, lowered the error of a two-dimensional model for the dipole moments and HOMO–LUMO gaps of 10,175 tmQM complexes from 1.68 to 1.24 D and from 0.367 to 0.311 eV. MeCoBi is open source, with a web interface at mecobi.york.ac.uk.

item.title: Boronium-Based Ionic Liquids: From an Unusual Main-Group Cation to Functional Ionic Materials
item.description: Boronium-based ionic liquids, sometimes referred to by the acronym “BILs”—are salts in which the cation is a tetra-coordinate, boron-centred molecular ion, and which occupy a distinctive intersection of main-group, coordination and ionic liquid chemistry. Their modern development largely began with robust L1L2BH2+ ions (L = Lewis-base ligand) and the recognition that appropriate ligand and anion choices can render these salts room-temperature liquids. Two decades of work now support a coherent materials picture involving them: nitrogen-donor boronium cations can combine low glass-transition or melting temperatures with useful ionic conductivity, wide electrochemical stability windows and exceptional resistance to reduction at lithium metal. These attributes have led to the creation of durable lithium-metal cells, high-voltage electrochemical double-layer capacitors, and polymerizable electrolyte platforms. Pairings with certain anions have yielded low-viscosity hypergolic fuels; deliberately lipophilic/amphiphilic structures have served as ashless lubricant additives, and can display antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral activity. Their structural variety has simultaneously expanded beyond canonical N,N-donor frameworks to cations in which ureas and amides serve as O-donor ligands, and to hydrolytically robust salts of +3 boronium ions. This review maps out chemically rigorous bounds for BILs, reconciles nomenclature and electronic-structure descriptions, surveys synthesis and property relationships, benchmarks the best-supported applications, and identifies places where data remains sparse. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing formal charge bookkeeping from the distributed charge of real cations, on avoiding an unsupported general description of B–H bonds as hydridic, and on separating useful screening metrics from device-level validation. The emerging design paradigm for these salts is not simply “put boron somewhere in an ionic liquid”; rather, it is to co-design donor set, cation shape, anion chemistry, interfacial reactivity and phase behaviour as one coupled system.

item.title: GPU-Accelerated Evaluation of MP2 Correlation Energy Densities for Machine Learning of Density Functionals
item.description: Second-order Møller–Plesset (MP2) correlation energy densities can serve as ingredients for machine learning (ML) of density functionals that improve upon MP2-based double hybrids. However, limitations of existing implementations have restricted the evaluation of these energy densities and of ML-based functionals employing them to small systems. Here, we develop a GPU-accelerated implementation for evaluating MP2 correlation energy densities and their regularized and spin-resolved variants by combining a density fitting scheme that preserves high pointwise accuracy with memory-efficient tensor contractions. We demonstrate the use of the resulting energy densities in ML-based density functional approximations (DFAs) through the previously developed MLS2 model [Nat. Commun. 16, 11306 (2025)] and limMLS2, a variant introduced here that enforces a high density limit constraint to MLS2. The GPU-accelerated evaluation of MP2 energy densities enables routine application of these ML-based DFAs to systems described by more than 5000 atomic orbitals, with predictions remaining robust to the density fitting approximations and grid sizes tested. Overall, by making MP2 correlation energy densities accessible for larger systems, our work broadens their use in the development and application of highly accurate ML-based DFAs.

item.title: AnCore: A Six-Stage Structure-Based Virtual Screening Pipeline Integrating Two-Phase Redocking, Reciprocal Rank Fusion Consensus Scoring, and a Contact-Anchored Elastic-Network Pose-Persistence Heuristic
item.description: Structure-based virtual screening workflows often keep molecular visualization apart from multi-engine consensus rescoring and post-docking triage. We present AnCore Scientific Studio (v1.2.0), an open-source macOS workbench that couples a Rust/Tauri shell and a 3Dmol.js viewport to a six-stage Python pipeline. The stages are (1) receptor curation with AMBER14/GBn2 minimization and a steric clash gate; (2) a two-phase co-crystal redocking gate, with local BFGS refinement (Phase A) and focused-box Monte Carlo search (Phase B); (3) RDKit ligand preparation; (4) consensus rescoring of AutoDock Vina, Vinardo and AutoDock4 by Reciprocal Rank Fusion and mean Z-score; (5) 3D radial interaction fingerprinting; and (6) post-docking triage, made up of unrestrained full-atom minimization (Mode A), a 3.0 ps contact-anchored elastic-network pose-persistence heuristic (Mode B) and export of 100-ns explicit-solvent OpenMM/GROMACS packages (Mode C). We tested the pipeline on a five-target development benchmark (1IEP, 3ERT, 1UYG, 1M17, 1STP; 50 ligands, 25 literature actives and 25 presumed-inactive decoys, plus 5 co-crystal references). All five co-crystal ligands passed the 2.00 Å redocking gate (mean RMSD 0.906 ± 0.388 Å). Consensus rescoring raised the suite-mean ROC-AUC from 0.584 for Vina alone to 0.696 for mean Z-score (one-sided paired bootstrap p = 0.0070). A contact-count control that uses no co-crystal information reached 0.864, and the Mode B heuristic reached 0.920. Because the Mode B parameters were set during development on these same targets, and because its inputs overlap with the contact counts it is compared against, we treat these two figures as in-sample results. Mode B also rejected 40% of the actives under hard cutoffs, so it should be used for ranking and not for rejection. Prospective validation on independent DUD-E and LIT-PCBA targets is still needed.
