item.title: Flat-band driven bipolar anomalous Nernst effect towards volt-scale transverse thermoelectric conversion
item.description: arXiv:2611.19039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unipolar anomalous Nernst thermopiles are critically plagued by metallic interconnects, which induce heavy Joule dissipation and compromise the module's packing density, ultimately capping voltage generation. Here, we circumvent these limitations by establishing an intrinsic bipolar anomalous Nernst effect (BANE) paradigm, enabling seamless series integration analogous to Seebeck n-p pairs without passive metallic bridges. Focusing on flat-band topological systems, through machine learning assisted screening across multiple target properties, we identified 249 BANE materials, exhibiting near-room-temperature polarity switching. Guided by this predictive framework, we experimentally realized this phenomenon in single crystals of the Weyl ferromagnet, Co$_2$TiGe. Strikingly, while its intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) remains rigorously temperature-invariant up to the Curie temperature, the anomalous Nernst signal undergoes a sharp polarity inversion across $T \approx 225$ K. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to the interplay between flat bands and Weyl nodes, where thermal depopulation shifts the chemical potential across the band edge, inverting the sign of $\partial \sigma_{xy} / \partial \epsilon$ via the Mott relation. This work opens an avenue toward compact, monolithic transverse thermopiles capable of volt-scale generation free from interfacial parasitic dissipation.

item.title: Exploring Energy Landscapes for Functional Materials: Ga vacancies in $\beta$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$
item.description: arXiv:2611.19365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy landscape exploration requires extensive energy and force evaluations, making efficient access to interatomic potentials an important practical challenge. We present a persistent socket interface that connects the landscape exploration tools in the GMIN, OPTIM, and PATHSAMPLE programs to potentials available through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). The persistent design keeps both the calculator and socket connection active throughout the search, avoiding repeated initialisation. We apply this framework to understand and predict the properties of Ga vacancies in $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ using two NequIP-based potentials, and construct kinetic transition networks describing complex vacancy configurations and migration pathways. Temperature-dependent analysis of the dominant paths reveals how the most probable migration sequence can change, with the mechanism governed by global properties of the network, rather than simply the highest energy barrier. Visualisation, mean first-passage times, and heat capacities enable us to connect the organisation of the landscape to relaxation time scales and thermodynamic observables. The interface extends energy landscape methods to ASE-compatible atomistic models, providing a general framework for combining global optimisation, transition state searches, kinetic network analysis, and thermodynamic characterisation with recent developments in machine-learned interatomic potentials.

item.title: Scaling laws in machine learning on non-ideal experimental data enable inverse design of radiative-cooling coatings
item.description: arXiv:2611.19596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials informatics increasingly targets multicomponent materials, yet experimental datasets inevitably contain non-ideal variations arising from imperfect uniformity and reproducibility in composition, coating formation, and measurement. Whether machine-learning prediction accuracy scales with amount of data under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we develop an automated platform that produced and optically characterized 11,520 radiative-cooling coatings spanning nine material and processing parameters. Forward and inverse neural networks, and a spectrum-conditioned diffusion model were trained on subsets of 10 to 10,000 samples. All models exhibited power-law scaling, with prediction errors decreasing with dataset size. Experimental inverse-design validation showed that larger datasets produced spectra closer to a broadband-emitter target. The diffusion model generated multiple candidate parameter sets, allowing selection among alternative solutions based on ease of fabrication, cost, and scalability. These results demonstrate predictable learning-curve scaling in non-ideal experimental data and provide a quantitative basis for estimating the benefit of additional experimental data, and thus the cost-effectiveness of materials-informatics.

item.title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
item.description: arXiv:2611.19793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

item.title: Mixed-Sign Kitaev Exchange in Jahn-Teller-Distorted CrI$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2611.19799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kitaev couplings with ferromagnetic (FM) or antiferromagnetic (AFM) character shape magnetic frustration and phases differently in real materials, yet their coexistence within a single material remains unexplored. Here, we propose Jahn-Teller distortion as a route to realizing such coexistence on inequivalent bonds. First-principles calculations identify monolayer CrI$_2$ as such a system, with AFM and FM Kitaev couplings on the short and long bonds, respectively. These opposite signs are robust against variations in Hubbard $U$, functionals, and strain. A minimal tight-binding model links this sign contrast to Jahn-Teller-split $t_{2g}$ orbitals and their hopping to $e_g$ orbitals. We further adopt the cluster expansion method and develop a realistic machine-learned spin Hamiltonian, which reproduces the experimentally observed proper-screw geometry and propagation direction and reveals highly nonuniform spin rotation, with turning angles ranging from $48.0^\circ$ to $93.9^\circ$. Both proper-screw anisotropy and strong anharmonic spin rotation arise from the mixed-sign Kitaev interaction. These findings not only establish Jahn-Teller distortion as a microscopic route to mixed-sign Kitaev exchange, but also open a new avenue for exploring novel magnetic phases.

item.title: Basic introduction to Freidlin-Wentzell theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.19916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Freidlin-Wentzell theory provides the quantitative foundation for rare, noise-induced transitions in stochastic dynamical systems, predicting optimal transition pathways, the exponential scaling of mean escape times, and the long-term occupancy of competing attractors in metastable systems. Here we present a pedagogical, physics-oriented review built around a unified Hamiltonian framework: starting from the infinitesimal generator of a continuous-time Markov process, we derive the local Hamiltonian, obtain the Lagrangian and action functional via Legendre-Fenchel duality, and construct the quasi-potential landscape. We apply this streamlined formalism across weak-noise diffusions, Markov jump processes, weakly interacting particle ensembles, and nonequilibrium stochastic fields, alongside exact conditions for macroscopic coarse-graining. Along the way, we highlight how broken detailed balance drives forward and reverse transition paths apart, explain where local linear stability and Gaussian approximations break down, and assemble multi-attractor landscapes using combinatorial $W$-graphs. Finally, we bridge the analytical theory to modern numerical solvers, including ordered upwind methods, geometric minimum action algorithms, and neural-network parameterizations, and provide an accompanying GPU-accelerated Python package.

item.title: Optical spin Edelstein response of d-wave altermagnets
item.description: arXiv:2611.20235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The momentum-dependent spin splitting and compensated magnetic order in altermagnets offer opportunities for electrical control of spin polarization. We explore the spin Edelstein effect in the frequency domain of a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet with Rashba spin-orbit coupling. We calculate the spin-velocity susceptibility response function beyond the intraband response regime and find that the interband longitudinal and transverse Edelstein responses are governed by the Zeeman quantum metric and Zeeman Berry curvature, respectively. The density of states presents a logarithmic van Hove singularity at exactly the negative value of the energy below which four disconnected Fermi contours emerge. This defines three distinctive regions for the position of the Fermi level, through which the Edelstein susceptibility tensor displays characteristic spectral features, reflecting the topological change of the Fermi surface. The resulting spin magnetization shows a strong dependence on the driving frequency and on the orientation of the in-plane external electric field. Our results highlight new possibilities for electrical and optical control of the spin Edelstein effect in altermagnets that could find spintronic applications.

item.title: Machine Learning the $GW$ Self-Energy Operator for Real Materials
item.description: arXiv:2611.20247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning of $GW$ in solids has largely focused on prediction of scalar quasiparticle energy corrections. Here, we introduce a phase-aware many-body transformer that predicts the full $\mathbf{k}$-resolved complex self-energy matrix. As a proof of principle, we apply the model to predict quasiparticle energies before and after diagonalization of the quasiparticle Hamiltonian, obtaining a test set mean absolute error (MAE) of 29 meV for a dataset of 1745 2D materials in the static COHSEX approximation and 60 meV for a more limited dataset of 433 materials calculated within a plasmon-pole model. COHSEX pretraining followed by finetuning reduces this MAE to 42 meV. The predicted matrices also accurately reproduce QP wavefunctions.

item.title: Oxygens breathe, electrons jump
item.description: arXiv:2611.20260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electronic transport in polyanionic battery cathodes proceeds through small-polaron hopping between transition-metal sites and is commonly assumed to be tightly coupled to the motion of charge-compensating mobile ions. Using olivine Li$_x$MnPO$_4$ as a prototypical platform, we use first-principles molecular dynamics with extended Hubbard functionals to follow, in real time and at finite temperature, the adiabatic evolution of Mn oxidation states and atomic sublattices. We find that polaron hopping and cation migration are dynamically decoupled: Mn$^{2+}$/Mn$^{3+}$ valence exchanges occur frequently while the intercalated ions remain confined to their sites, and hopping is gated by the local oxygen framework. Freezing the six oxygen atoms of an individual MnO$_6$ octahedron excludes that site from the hopping network, while increasing the fictitious oxygen mass slows down electronic transport. Each valence exchange coincides with a concerted breathing of the donor and acceptor octahedra ($\Delta V \simeq 2$ $\r{A}^3$), with their volume asymmetry crossing zero at the transition, consistent with the Holstein-Marcus coincidence condition. The hopping rate yields an activation energy of $E_a = 0.20 \pm 0.03$ eV, closely matching the elastic energy scale of the two coordination cages ($\lambda_V/4 \approx 0.20$ eV). These results identify the oxygen coordination cage, not the mobile cation sublattice, as the dynamical gate for small-polaron transport: a site can accept the electron only if its cage can breathe, and the barrier is governed by cage elasticity. Selective constraints and mass scaling applied to first-principles dynamics provide a general route to link electronic and lattice degrees of freedom in redox-active materials, opening the door to framework engineering in intercalation and mixed ionic-electronic conductors.

item.title: Scaling a Universal Graph Neural Network Force Field to Billions of Atoms on Desk-Side GPUs
item.description: arXiv:2611.20585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning force fields are capable of simulating billions of atoms, but usually require high-performance supercomputing clusters. We show that a universal graph neural network force field, ALIGNN-FF, evaluates energies and forces of more than one billion atoms on desk-side computers such as the NVIDIA GB10, which has 128 GB of unified memory, by using a cube-and-halo decomposition. The halo contains every atom within the model's 20 {\AA} receptive field, which makes the result exact. One GB10 holds 216,000 atoms with forces as a single graph. The cube-and-halo decomposition removes this limit, enabling an evaluation of 2 billion atoms on nine GB10s. We also demonstrate three case studies: a billion-atom polycrystal, a 102-million-atom microelectronic gate stack and a 1.07-million-atom satellite tobacco mosaic virus in water. This brings single-point evaluations at experimentally relevant sizes within reach of one research group. The code is available at: https://github.com/atomgptlab/scalingmat.

item.title: Bias Conditioning and Long-Range Electrostatics for Consistent Machine-Learning Potentials of Electrified Interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.21026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) of electrified interfaces need the bias as input, but it is unclear whether a scalar electrode charge suffices and whether short-range models capture the non-local response. We add charge and field conditioning to short- and long-range MLIPs. State-of-the-art field-conditioned short-range models overpolarize thick water films nearly twofold and miss work-function shifts at stepped Pt. Our long-range model captures both, needs only the electrode charge at metals as input, and reproduces ab initio simulations of the Pt(111)--water interface.

item.title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
item.description: arXiv:2611.21147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

item.title: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.21398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. We show that self-attention is a real-space Dyson iteration whose Boltzmann (softmax) kernel acts as a two-body self-energy. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, L\"owdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.

item.title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
item.description: arXiv:2611.18588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening. Beyond literature screening, the framework extracts structured information from full-text articles, enabling content-level quantification of research landscapes that extends traditional bibliometric analysis based on publication metadata. This capability reveals methodological trends and underexplored directions, as shown for machine learning in concrete materials science. We further demonstrate its utility for information and data discovery by identifying publications containing silicate glass density data that are difficult to retrieve using conventional search strategies, which can support downstream hypothesis development, research design, and data-driven scientific discovery. Overall, these results demonstrate the broad applicability of LLM-powered literature analysis across scientific domains and its potential to transform large, unstructured literature corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge at scale.

item.title: A Beginner's Guide to Physical Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.18758v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Network theory studies entities (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges). While these entities and their relationships may be abstract in general, this tutorial focuses on the special case of physical networks: spatially embedded networks that carry physical quantities such as electric charge, fluid volume, or momentum. The underlying structure is described mathematically by a graph (Section I), with the incidence matrix playing a central role in the analysis. Viewing a graph as a special case of a cell complex reveals the topological structure of the incidence matrix and its relation to familiar operators from calculus (Section II). Because these networks are physical, flows are conserved at each node and often derive from the gradient of a potential. Models that satisfy these principles behave analogously to circuits; accordingly, we first review circuit theory (Section III), then examine related fluid flow (Section IV) and mechanical (Section V) networks. Briefly, the topics of random walkers (Section VI) and nonlinear networks (Section VII) will be discussed, followed by concluding remarks (Section VIII). Analytical examples and Python implementations, in lieu of pseudocode, are included throughout. Exercises are included as footnotes. This tutorial is based on a short course taught at the Boulder School for Condensed Matter in 2019 and a course taught at the University of Pennsylvania in Spring 2024. It should be a useful resource for students, teachers, and researchers applying graph theory to physical networks. Knowledge of linear algebra is assumed, but no prior knowledge of graph theory or physics is necessary.

item.title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
item.description: arXiv:2611.19614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

item.title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.19658v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

item.title: Matching two-dimensional statistics does not certify three-dimensional transport in battery electrodes
item.description: arXiv:2611.20121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Three-dimensional battery electrode structures reconstructed from two-dimensional micrographs are routinely used to predict transport, assuming that matching the measured 2D statistics reproduces the relevant 3D properties. We test this premise on X-ray tomograms of three all-solid-state cathodes. With a differentiable conductivity solver, we optimise voxel structures that match the real electrode in phase fractions, boundary density, two- and three-point correlations and lineal-path functions, on all section planes, slab by slab and layer by layer, within measurement noise. Every sample has statistical twins conducting 10-88-fold less than the real electrode, robust to 5^3 majority filtering, whereas the most conductive are at most 3.3-fold above it. The twins rearrange rather than remove material, severing or funnelling through-plane paths. A classifier on 2D sections detects them, as it does current 2D-to-3D generators: the information is in the images but not in the statistics. Matching standard 2D statistics therefore does not certify 3D transport.

item.title: GPRidge: Gaussian-process Accelerated Calculations of Minimum Energy Paths and First-order Saddle Points
item.description: arXiv:2611.20591v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GPRidge, a Gaussian-process (GP) library for accelerating calculations of minimum energy paths and first-order saddle points with compiled-language and Python bindings, is presented. An evaluation controller uses GP predictions to iteratively adjust the Cartesian coordinates of the atoms. The fitted GP energy surface and measured energies and forces pass from the path calculation to local refinement of the saddle point. New evaluations improve the surrogate and check the candidate geometry. For the molecular calculations, acceptance requires measured-force convergence and an independent Hessian with only one negative eigenvalue. A second negative eigenvalue triggers an escape and renewed refinement. The controller supports a joint inverse-distance GP for molecules and local GP residuals on periodic systems. Applications to the 24 Baker-Chan and 20 Birkholz-Schlegel molecular reactions using the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA-S-1.1), and to 72 Pt heptamer and island rearrangements on Pt(111) using a Morse potential, are presented. On matched Baker-Chan reactions, GPRidge uses 7.8- and 7.0-fold fewer energy-and-force evaluations than climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) and off-path climbing-image nudged elastic band (OCI-NEB), respectively, reducing validation-inclusive CI-NEB time by 41%. All 20 Birkholz-Schlegel saddle points pass the independent index-one check, compared with 17 for the classical dimer method started from the same path maxima; on those 17 reactions, the GP dimer stage uses 6.4-fold fewer evaluations. All 72 Pt(111) paths meet the OptBench force criterion, with median evaluation counts of 30 and 23 for the heptamer and island problems, against 778 and 443 for CI-NEB.

item.title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
item.description: arXiv:2611.21116v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.

item.title: Storage and Learning phase transitions in the Random-Features Hopfield Model
item.description: arXiv:2303.16880v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Hopfield model is a paradigmatic model of neural networks that has been analyzed for many decades in the statistical physics, neuroscience, and machine learning communities. Inspired by the manifold hypothesis in machine learning, we propose and investigate a generalization of the standard setting that we name Random-Features Hopfield Model. Here $P$ binary patterns of length $N$ are generated by applying to Gaussian vectors sampled in a latent space of dimension $D$ a random projection followed by a non-linearity. Using the replica method from statistical physics, we derive the phase diagram of the model in the limit $P,N,D\to\infty$ with fixed ratios $\alpha=P/N$ and $\alpha_D=D/N$. Besides the usual retrieval phase, where the patterns can be dynamically recovered from some initial corruption, we uncover a new phase where the features characterizing the projection can be recovered instead. We call this phenomena the learning phase transition, as the features are not explicitly given to the model but rather are inferred from the patterns in an unsupervised fashion.

item.title: jahn-teller-dynamics: Python package to determine vibronic interaction demonstrated on molecules and trigonal defect qubits
item.description: arXiv:2512.05704v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trigonal solid-state defects are often subjects of spontaneous symmetry breaking driven by the $E\otimes e$ Jahn-Teller effect, reflecting strong electron-phonon coupling. These systems, particularly paramagnetic defect qubits in solids are central for quantum technology applications, where accurate knowledge of their fine-structure parameters - shaped by the complex interplay of spin-orbit and electron-phonon interactions - is essential. We introduce the $\mathtt{jahn {\text -} teller {\text -} dynamics}$ package, a Python code that implements the first-principles approach of [Phys. Rev. X 8, 021063 (2018)] to accurately compute the spin-orbit-phonon entanglement in trigonal defects utilizing the output from density functional theory calculations (DFT) to predict fine-structure parameters of zero-phonon lines (ZPLs), including Zeeman shifts under external magnetic fields. We demonstrate its capabilities on negatively charged Group-IV-vacancy (G4V) defects in diamond: SiV$^-$, GeV$^-$, SnV$^-$, PbV$^-$ and the neutral N$_3$V$^0$ defect in diamond, and the CH$_3$O$^0$ methoxy radical. Additionally, we implement a generic electron-phonon code that is capable entangling an arbitrary amount of (i) vibration modes and (ii) electronic levels by (iii) arbitrarily high order of vibronic interaction terms. Exemplarily, we demonstrate the Jahn-Teller multimode problem on the CH$_3$O$^0$ methoxy radical and the Pseudo Jahn-Teller case on the $C_4H_4^+$ butatrien cation.

item.title: Prescreening Point Defects in Semiconductors With Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.14846v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-throughput calculations using density-functional theory (DFT) are commonly used to explore point defects for applications in power electronics and quantum technologies. There is currently a major shift away from these traditional simulation techniques towards machine learning (ML) methods. We explore a class of physics-guided ML models for predicting defect formation energies and zero-phonon lines (ZPL) to identify point defects for quantum applications. The models are specifically targeted for use in a prescreening step for accelerated high-throughput workflows, and are therefore designed to avoid the costly relaxation step typically present with ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs). We compare performance for single and double point defect systems in 4H-SiC with ridge, kernel ridge, and multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using three different descriptors representing the defect systems. For vacancies and substitutions, the optimized models give mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 0.478 eV for the formation energy and 0.202 eV for ZPLs, which is just above the level at which such predictions can be useful even beyond the targeted prescreening, i.e., in some applications they may completely replace the need for costly DFT calculations. For interstitials the MAEs are larger, 1.123 eV for the formation energy and 0.230 eV for the ZPL, which, while still useful for prescreening, will not generally be useful for more detailed characterization. Hence, while the results may be further improved by model design and optimization, the models presented in this work are already useful for prescreening in high-throughput characterization of point defects.

item.title: Ultra-small-angle graphene twistronics with monolayer spacers: From interlayer hybridisation and moir\'e effects to high-temperature magnetotransport oscillations
item.description: arXiv:2610.08505v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Based on the analysis of moir\'e superlattice characteristics and interlayer hybridisation in small-angle twisted graphene multilayers with a monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spacer, we predict spectral features and quantum transport effects in these systems. Here, we consider both a twisted bilayer and double bilayers with a spacer, discuss double bilayers in two stacking orders - with and without inversion symmetry - and also compare the results obtained with self-consistent Hartree calculations with and without in-plane periodic charge distribution, offering computationally efficient models for these graphene/hBN/graphene moir\'e systems. We note parametric intervals where the appearance of minibands can be enhanced by tuning with an out-of-plane displacement field, and identify the miniband edges and van Hove singularities across a broad range of densities and displacement fields. These system host Lifshitz transitions at which the Fermi lines form a network across moir\'e Brillouin zones, and to which Brown-Zak oscillations converge at low magnetic field and elevated temperatures. We analyse interlayer hybridisation across the same parameter space, discuss how hybridisation affects in-plane magneto-transport in ultra-high-mobility structures, and predict that semiclassical magneto-oscillations of interlayer hybridisation can lead to 1/B-periodic quantum oscillations of resistivity persistent to high temperature.

item.title: Multi-Fidelity Machine Learning for Predicting Startup Stress Growth and Strain Hardening in Wormlike Micellar Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.04115v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wormlike micellar solutions exhibit formulation-dependent nonlinear startup responses, including stress overshoot, undershoot, and strain hardening, making prediction across compositions and shear rates challenging. We developed a multi-fidelity machine-learning framework to predict stress-growth curves in cetylpyridinium chloride (CPyCl)-based wormlike micelles from sparse experimental measurements. The framework combines a low-fidelity analytical model describing the overall startup response with high-fidelity experimental data capturing formulation-specific nonlinear features. This approach addresses the limited and uneven coverage of salt chemistry, concentration, and shear rate without relying solely on data-intensive neural-network training. The trained model predicts complete stress-growth responses at untested shear rates and enables extraction of strain-hardening characteristics from interpolated curves. By augmenting sparse rheological measurements, the framework provides a basis for exploring relationships among formulation variables, linear viscoelastic properties, and nonlinear startup behavior, while supporting more efficient characterization of wormlike micellar solutions.

item.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na3PS4
item.description: arXiv:2611.04547v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described as cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder shapes mesoscale transport remains unresolved. Using Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy on a micrometer-sized ball-milled Na3PS4 particle, we find that the host is not static. The cubic phase behaves as a strain glass of three degenerate tetragonal variants whose domain walls move under residual milling stress, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing. Rearrangements occur as scale-free avalanches, as in ferroelastic martensites but without external driving, while the tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics evolve on timescales comparable to ionic diffusion across the particle. This work introduces a probe of dynamics in locally frustrated solid electrolytes, revealing that mechanochemical synthesis yields not merely a metastable polymorph, but a stress-driven strain glass.

item.title: Harmonic origin of local symmetry breaking in PbTe revealed using machine-learned potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.12598v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We use machine-learned interatomic potentials combined with higher-order interatomic force constant models to show that finite-range polar correlations in PbTe are driven by long-range harmonic interactions rather than lattice anharmonicity. Our molecular dynamics simulations reveal a spatial polar correlation range exceeding 50 {\AA} at low temperatures and decreasing with increasing temperature. Selective interatomic force constant mapping demonstrates that crystal anharmonicity usually associated with the formation of polar nanoregions suppresses polar correlations. Instead, long-range harmonic interactions extending to 13 {\AA} are necessary to reproduce the spatial coherence of local dipoles. In reciprocal space, these extended harmonic interactions correspond to high curvature of the transverse optical (TO) phonon branch at the $\Gamma$ point. Comparison with isostructural NaCl connects these extended interactions to local underscreening of predominantly Coulombic forces. Our results provide a key microscopic description of finite-range polar correlations and a framework for understanding local symmetry breaking in centrosymmetric materials.

item.title: AI-Enabled Qubit Loss Detection and Replenishment Strategy for Atom Array Quantum Computing
item.description: arXiv:2604.14269v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Qubit loss is a major source of error in atom-array quantum computing and invalidates the algebraic structure of the standard stabilizer formalism for quantum error-correcting codes. On the one hand, it complicates decoding; on the other hand, it introduces tochastic flicker patterns in stabilizers as a hallmark of qubit loss. Here, we develop an artificial-intelligence-enabled decoder based on a spatiotemporal graph neural network (STGNN) architecture to extract spatial and temporal correlations from syndrome histories. Our decoder performs a dual-head task, simultaneously correcting standard Pauli errors and identifying the locations of qubit loss. Our decoder achieves significantly higher logical accuracy than both the traditional minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) algorithm and even delayed-erasure MWPM decoders that use qubit-loss information from the final round as input. Furthermore, we integrate the decoder into a sliding-window framework for dynamic qubit replenishment. We emphasize that our approach does not involve any additional physical measurements beyond stabilizer measurements, and detects qubit loss and determines its replacement strategy through a purely software-based AI policy. We demonstrate that our approach bounds the accumulation of lost qubits and fully restores the fault-tolerant scaling behavior. For realistic near-term error rates, this work provides a robust and scalable framework for correcting qubit-loss errors, paving the way for more efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation.

item.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.07998v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

item.title: A stopping rule for completing computed phase diagrams with generative models
item.description: Phase diagrams constructed using known phases misjudge stability when key phases are missing. Generative models supply as many structures as needed, but how many structures to generate and which diagrams will change are unknown. We add 10,000 MatterGen structures per system, relaxed with a machine learning interatomic potential, to Materials Project (MP) data for six Li–transition-metal–O ternaries and track the hull convergence. The responses fall into two groups: Li–Ru–O, Li–Hf–O, and Li–Zr–O (70–107 MP structures) gain 4–9 stable candidates and exhibit total convex-hull shifts of 59.9–62.9 meV/atom, whereas Li–Mn–O, Li–Co–O, and Li–Ni–O (240–609) exhibit a minimal hull shift. When reduced to 70 MP structures, the latter gain a similar number of stable candidates by rediscovering removed hull phases. The hulls converge within 5,000–8,000 structures. After generating 8,000 structures, a stopping rule, tested using Li–Ir–O, decides whether more are needed. Density functional theory places seven Li–Ru–O compositions 5–83 meV/atom below the MP-only hull but rejects the potential’s false positives in well-explored systems. This gives a stopping rule and early diagnostic for incomplete phase diagrams.

item.title: Transforming spinel LiMn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> into a Na-layered cathode
item.description:
Nature Communications, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79390-z

Spinel LiMn2O4 has potential to be transformed into a layered Na-storage material, but the mechanism remains unclear. Here, authors investigate the ion migration mechanism during the transformation and evaluate the Na storage performance of the resulting material, including application in pouch and cylindrical cells.

item.title: Metal-oxo clusters stabilize electron-selective interfaces for efficient perovskite solar cells
item.description: Efficient perovskite photovoltaics require durable interfaces compatible with scalable manufacturing. Solution-processable metal-oxo clusters combine robust inorganic frameworks with tunable organic components to enhance charge extraction and suppress ion migration. Complementary clusters stabilize both interfaces of the electron-transport layer, enabling a certified efficiency of 26.7% and improved operational stability. This modular strategy links molecular interface engineering with scalable coating, offering a pathway toward efficient, durable perovskite solar technologies.

item.title: Dynamic staged solid electrolyte interphase via sequential chemical and electrochemical reactions for highly reversible zinc battery
item.description: Fluorinated cations and anions are incorporated to synergistically restructure the EDL architecture, thereby enabling the formation of a dynamic staged SEI with an organic upper and an inorganic-rich inner via chemical and electrochemical reactions. The preferential adsorption of FPy+ cations promotes adsorption of the OTF− anion at the EDL, thereby engineering an EDL architecture with low active water. This not only facilitates the formation of a dynamic staged SEI film but also effectively mitigates interfacial side reactions.

item.title: Artificial intelligence-driven multispectral camouflage technologies
item.description: The rise of multi-band detection systems has revealed the critical shortcomings of single- or narrow-band camouflage, driving an urgent demand for advanced multispectral camouflage technologies. Micro- and nanophotonics facilitate tremendous breakthroughs in precise spectral control, paving the way for effective multispectral camouflage applications. However, progress in precise spectral engineering has long been impeded by the inherent bottlenecks of intuition-based design approaches. Concurrently, the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) offers powerful and innovative approaches for designing and optimizing photonic structures and metamaterials, heralding a revolution in photonics research. Recently, AI-driven computational inverse design methodologies, which tailor high-performance photonic structures from desired functionalities, have rapidly emerged and been successfully applied to multispectral camouflage. Consequently, the integration of AI with multispectral camouflage technologies represents a promising strategy to surpass conventional configurations and accelerate progress in this domain. This review begins with the elucidation of spectral requirements for multispectral camouflage and methodologies underpinning typical AI algorithms, continues with the optimization of photonic structures in multispectral camouflage via optimization algorithms, proceeds to advances in novel machine learning models for enhancing the efficiency of structural design and optimization, and finally concludes with a forward-looking commentary on challenges and perspectives in this evolving field.

item.title: GBProject: A comprehensive database of fundamental grain-boundary properties in metals
item.description: Artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML)-driven materials design through grain-boundary (GB) engineering has emerged as a promising strategy for developing next-generation metals and alloys. However, its broader application has been limited by the lack of comprehensive GB databases needed to train robust AI/ML models for accurately predicting GB structures and properties across diverse crystallographic and chemical spaces. In this study, we develop a comprehensive GB database through high-throughput atomistic simulations of 28 elemental metals using both semi-empirical and machine-learning interatomic potentials. The current dataset contains 3519 face-centered cubic, 3910 body-centered cubic, and 315 hexagonal close-packed GBs, spanning four representative GB types: symmetric-tilt, twist, asymmetric-tilt, and mixed (tilt–twist) GBs. All GB structures are generated using a coincident-site lattice-based workflow implemented in the open-access Grain-Boundary Project website (GBProject.org). For each GB, two key interfacial properties, including GB excess free energy and free volume, are systematically calculated. Both the optimized GB structures and the associated property data are publicly available through the GBProject website. This GB database provides a reliable and reusable resource for validating theoretical models, benchmarking atomistic simulations, and evaluating state-of-the-art foundation models for large-scale GB simulations. It also establishes a solid foundation for developing advanced AI/ML models to accelerate the design of polycrystalline materials.

item.title: Mesoporous Separator Engineering Rectified Electrolyte Chemistry for Durable Non-Aqueous Aluminium-Ion Batteries
item.description: Rechargeable non-aqueous aluminium-ion batteries (AIBs) are promising low-cost and sustainable energy storage systems, but their development is hindered by sluggish transport of strongly associated chloroaluminate ions and unstable aluminium plating/stripping. Here we demonstrate that engineering the separator microenvironment effectively regulates electrolyte chemistry and interfacial ion transport in AIBs. A binder-free dendritic mesoporous silicamodified glass fiber (DMS-GF) separator is developed by growing DMS nanoparticles directly 2 at the GF scaffold surface. The resulting silanol-rich mesoporous architecture weakens anioncation interactions in chloroaluminate electrolytes, promotes ion dissociation, and shifts electrolyte speciation towards the electrochemically active Al2Cl7 - species, leading to enhanced ionic mobility. The interconnected mesoporous channels further homogenise ion transport and electrolyte distribution, enabling highly reversible and stable aluminium plating/stripping with suppressed dendrite growth. In graphene//Al full batteries, the DMS-GF separator enables high reversible capacity, improved rate capability, and long-term cycling stability, outperforming pristine GF separators. This work demonstrates that separator microenvironment engineering can synchronously regulate electrolyte chemistry and interfacial electrochemical processes for high-performance AIBs, providing a promising strategy for controlling ion transport in unconventional battery systems.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Network Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling end-to-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. For a feed-forward neural network (FNN) using extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs), embedding the EoS reduces the average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 8.67% to 5.57%. Replacing the FNN and ECFP representation with a graph neural network (GNN) using cyclic polymer graphs further reduces the average MAPE to 2.58%. Pre-training the models on PC-SAFT parameters for small molecules, followed by fine-tuning on polymer PVT data, yields additional improvements, reducing the average MAPE to 5.06% for the FNN and 2.15% for the GNN. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining an embedded EoS with geometric deep learning and transfer learning for accurate polymer PVT predictions.

item.title: How Chemical Evidence Shapes Mechanistic Reasoning and Prediction by Large Language Models: Fine-Grained Inference in Nucleoside-Derived Supramolecular Gelation
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) offer a distinctive capability for chemical problem solving by integrating chemical knowledge and experimental evidence through reasoning expressed in natural language. Yet how chemical evidence reshapes their predictions and expressed rationales is not self-evident and has received limited examination, particularly for challenging chemical problems. Here, using nucleoside-derived supramolecular gelation as a testbed, we systematically varied the evidence provided to LLMs and quantitatively evaluated their predictions and the mechanistic alignment of generated rationales. Without additional evidence, correct predictions were associated with greater alignment to literature-supported mechanisms than incorrect ones, suggesting that LLMs can draw on intrinsic chemical knowledge despite rationales remain largely general. Structurally similar gelation precedents, thought improved prediction accuracy significantly, reduced this distinction by anchoring rationales to insufficiently discriminative structural features, indicating that similarity-based evidence does not necessarily improve chemical reasoning and that prediction accuracy alone is insufficient to assess LLM performance in chemical tasks. In contrast, condition-constrained references and mechanistic information more consistently directed rationales toward chemically discriminative features, even when prediction accuracy did not improve in tandem. Together, our study highlights the importance of task-specific evidence design and quantitative rationale evaluation for reliable chemical problem solving by LLMs.

item.title: Short-circuit-resistant sulfide solid-state batteries through lithium dewetting
item.description: In sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries, lithium dendrites penetrate the solid electrolyte indiscriminately through grain boundaries, interparticle voids and pores, causing internal short circuits that accelerate degradation and terminate cell life. This penetration has been understood largely in mechanical terms, and mitigation has focused on suppressing cracks. Here we show that chemical wetting, governed by the lithium/electrolyte interfacial energy, is a decisive factor in lithium penetration. Even when crack pathways were mechanically suppressed, short circuits persisted, because the negative interfacial energy renders sulfide electrolytes lithium-wetting, drawing lithium into their pores. Incorporating a small amount of tungsten, which strongly repels lithium, induced lithium dewetting and suppressed infiltration. The resulting electrolyte sustained lithium plating and stripping for more than two years without short circuiting and enabled long-lived high-rate full cells and anode-less pouch cells under low stack pressure. These findings establish interfacial energy as a key design parameter for durable all-solid-state batteries.

item.title: What we know and what we don’t: an audit of experimental solid-electrolyte data, and the patent literature as an untapped source
item.description: Machine-learning (ML) models for solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are trained on experimental ionic-conductivity data, yet public datasets are smaller, more duplicated and noisier than their sizes suggest. We merged the five open Li conductivity datasets we could download (Liverpool Ionics, Laskowski et al., McHaffie et al., OBELiX and the text-mined set of Shon and Min) and audited them in three ways. First, after re-extracting one dataset from its PDF table, normalising compositions and collapsing copies, the four curated datasets shrink from 3,336 nominal entries to 1,481 unique compositions from 540 papers; the CSV rendering most users would download hides a fifth of them. 86% of OBELiX records are exact copies of records in its parent datasets. Second, for 194 compositions reported by two or more papers, the median spread is 3.4-fold, and a report lies on average 0.43 log units from its composition median, nearly three times the spread among eight laboratories measuring identical powder. A systematic offset per paper accounts for 85% of this between-paper variation, and phase labels explain much of the largest spreads, while activation energies vary between papers no more than between laboratories. Third, one gradient-boosting model scores a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.90 log units under random cross-validation, 1.20–1.42 when entries from the same paper are kept together, 1.89 on a time split and 2.24 when a structure family is held out, worse than predicting the median; five other learners show the same pattern. Concatenating public datasets without deduplication lets copies leak into test folds and lowers the random-split MAE to 0.57, close to the experimental spread. We also built and tested a pipeline that extracts composition–conductivity records with evidence quotes from 100 recent patents in CPC H01M 10/0562. One in five reports measured conductivities, and these documents hold 171 distinct lithium compositions, 92% of them absent from the open datasets; halides make up a third of them against 4% of the literature set, and garnet and perovskite oxides are missing. Against a 25-patent reference set the pipeline recovers about half of the table records at a precision of 0.84; the reference set was drafted by the extraction model and has not yet been checked by hand, so these scores are provisional. We recommend a minimum reporting standard for conductivity, published duplicate maps and versions for datasets, group-aware splits reported against the experimental spread, and release of patent-derived facts with citations only.
